sazan-kushner.story:
Sazan is Albania's largest island, a strip of rock in the Adriatic Sea about 4.8 km long and 2 km wide, with an area of 5.7 square kilometres. It sits between the Strait of Otranto and the Bay of Vlorë, where the Adriatic meets the Ionian Sea, and that position has made it valuable to armies. For decades Albania's then-ally the Soviet Union used it as a submarine base and as a testing ground for biological and chemical weapons, and Soviet-era gas masks still lie around the island. It remains a designated military exclusion zone, nobody lives there, and it has been open to the public only since July 2015.

Across the water is Zvërnec, a strip of beach and cliffs that shelters an inland lagoon. It belongs to a protected area called Vjosa-Narta, where the ornithologist Taulant Bino and his colleagues have recorded about 250 bird species, including flamingos and breeding terns.

Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, the son-in-law and daughter of US President Donald Trump, want to build a luxury resort here. Ivanka Trump said in a 2026 podcast that they found Sazan years ago while on a friend's boat, swam ashore and hiked to the top. She described both the island and about five miles of beachfront opposite it as theirs. Bino says the project ideas he has seen show tall buildings and up to 10,000 rooms, which he describes as a new city.

The legal path ran through Albania's parliament. Land in a protected area normally cannot be used this way. Dorian Matlija, a lawyer for a group of environmental organizations, says the area's rules allow only traditional farming and fishing. In 2024 Prime Minister Edi Rama's government passed a law that removed the area's protection and allowed five-star hotels, and the government has given the resort preliminary approval. The environmental groups have gone to court. They argue that the law breaks Albanian law and also the rules of Natura 2000, the European Union's network of protected nature sites, which they say bind Albania because it is a candidate to join the EU.

Construction crews built an access road into the protected area during the breeding season. In June 2026 thousands protested outside the prime minister's office in Tirana for days on end, and hundreds gathered on the beach itself. Some said that the government was selling land that was not its to sell.

The money is hard to trace. On 2 June 2026 anti-corruption prosecutors froze the bank accounts of Albania Land Development, a firm owned by the Qatari brothers Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, who are helping to finance and build the resort, as part of an inquiry into fraudulent property titles. A representative said that Kushner's investment firm, Affinity Partners, has no role and that partners invest in their personal capacity. The investigative journalist Lindita Cela followed the ownership through a chain of shell companies, firms with no real business of their own, from Albania to the Netherlands. Several shared one Amsterdam address and were each worth a single euro.

Nothing here makes Sazan a separate country. Albania keeps the right to make and enforce law on the island and the beach, and a buyer gets only what Albanian law allows. The case shows the limit of that position for anyone hoping to build a private enclave. The permission rests on one government's statute, and the same courts, prosecutors and voters can reopen it. The resort is not finished, and the court cases and the title inquiry are unresolved.

singapore-1819-treaty.story:
Singapore is an island at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, beside the Strait of Malacca, the narrow sea lane that ships use between India and China. In the early 1800s it was part of the lands of the Sultanate of Johor. This entry is about the 1819 agreement that let a British trading company set up there, which Singapore officially treats as its modern founding. It matters to the story of founding territory because it shows how a private company could get a foothold on someone else's territory by paying local rulers, and how a right to trade could later grow into a right to rule.

The British had a commercial reason. Trade with China was growing and their ships needed bases along the route. In 1795, during wars in Europe, the exiled Dutch ruler told Dutch colonies to place themselves in British care, and Britain held places such as Malacca for some years. In 1814 Britain agreed to hand them back. The Dutch then charged heavy taxes on ships in their ports, British ships included, so the East India Company, the private British company that ran much of Britain's trade in Asia, began looking for a base of its own.

Stamford Raffles, a company official who governed the post of Bencoolen in Sumatra, persuaded the governor in India in 1818 to back a search. He landed at Singapore on 28 January 1819 and met the Temenggong, Abdul Rahman, the local noble who kept order there. Two days later they signed a provisional agreement. The Temenggong answered to the Sultan of Johor, though, and that created a problem. The reigning sultan, also called Abdul Rahman, had just made a deal with the Dutch and would not sign. Raffles used an old family quarrel to get around him. When the previous sultan died in 1811, his elder son Tengku Hussein was away at his own wedding, the younger son took the throne, and Hussein went into exile. Raffles had Hussein brought to Singapore and proclaimed him the rightful sultan.

On 6 February 1819 Raffles, Sultan Hussein and the Temenggong signed the treaty in a public ceremony. It allowed the company to keep a factory, the old word for a trading post, on the rulers' lands. The company would pay 5,000 Spanish dollars a year to the Sultan and 3,000 to the Temenggong. The two men promised not to make a treaty with any other nation or let any other European or American power settle.

Soon afterwards both men wrote to the Dutch and to the Yang di-Pertuan Muda of Riau, a senior regional official, saying that they had been forced to sign. On 1 March the British made them sign a statement of consent, and the Temenggong said his complaint had only been meant to head off Dutch retaliation. The British kept the post. In August 1824 a new treaty, drafted by the British official John Crawfurd, made the two rulers give up their full authority over Singapore and nearby islands in return for money allowances and the right to keep their property there.

The legal point is the difference between the two treaties. The 1819 paper bought permission to trade and a promise to keep rivals out, and the rulers still held the right to govern. Only the 1824 paper passed that right. The case also shows that a treaty is only as solid as the signer's title, and that Raffles got the title he needed by choosing which brother to call sultan.

state-to-state-purchases.story:
A government holds more than ownership of land. It holds sovereignty, the legal right to make and enforce law over a territory. For centuries rulers treated that right as something that could be sold, and this entry gathers the recorded sales. A sale of this kind is done by treaty. Once it is complete, the buyer's laws apply, and people's ordinary land titles may carry on underneath.

The list is long and goes back to the Middle Ages. Scotland paid Norway 4,000 marks sterling, plus a yearly 100 marks, for the Isle of Man and the Hebrides in 1266. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, about $7 per square kilometre, and Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867, about $4 per square kilometre. Brazil paid Bolivia £2 million for Acre in 1903. The United States paid Denmark $25 million for the 400 square kilometres of the Danish West Indies in 1916, or $62,500 per square kilometre, and in the same deal recognised Danish sovereignty over all of Greenland. The last sale on the list is Gwadar, a port that Pakistan bought from Muscat and Oman for £3 million in 1958. The prices are those of the time and are not adjusted for inflation. The list counts only transfers where money was paid for the territory itself, so it leaves out leases and payments for other purposes, such as war damages.

Every buyer and every seller on the list is a state or a ruler, and no private person or company appears. That matters to anyone who dreams of buying a piece of the world and running it. A private buyer can buy land and hold a deed, as anyone can, but the deed gives ownership under the seller's law. The seller's police, courts and tax office still apply. To get sovereignty a buyer would need other governments to accept that it now rules there, and the list shows no case of that happening for a private buyer.

Greenland shows how the idea survives and where it stops. In 2019 Donald Trump, then in his first term as US president, said he wanted the United States to buy Greenland, and the Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, called the idea absurd. In his second term he returned to it, and Danish and Greenlandic leaders answered that Greenland is not for sale and that its people have the right to decide their own future. The Greenlandic government stated that it chooses the Danish Realm over the United States. The right of a people to decide their own status has become part of how such a transfer is judged, which earlier sales ignored. No territory has been sold between states on this list since 1958.

sulu-heirs-arbitration.story:
Sabah is the Malaysian state that covers the northern tip of the island of Borneo. In the 1800s the Sultanate of Sulu, a Muslim kingdom based in islands now in the southern Philippines, claimed it. In 1878 the sultan signed a paper with Gustavus Baron de Overbeck, whose interests passed to the private British North Borneo Company. The sultan either ceded or leased the land, a point never settled because the wording has been read both ways, and the company agreed to pay him and his heirs a yearly fee. The paper also said any dispute would go to Her Britannic Majesty's Consul-General for Borneo, a British official.

The payments kept going long after the company and the empire had gone. Malaysia was formed in 1963 and, as the successor, went on paying the heirs. It stopped after the 2013 Lahad Datu standoff, when armed followers of a Sulu claimant entered Sabah and fought Malaysian forces.

In July 2019 eight people who say they descend from the sultan, all described by Malaysia as Philippine citizens, started arbitration in Spain. Arbitration is a private hearing where an appointed person decides a dispute in place of a court. It normally works only if both sides have agreed to use it, because its force comes from that agreement. Malaysia said it had not agreed. It argued that the consul-general's post no longer exists and that its own courts had taken over the role.

The Spanish arbitrator, Gonzalo Stampa, accepted the appointment and in May 2020 gave the heirs a partial award. In June 2021 the Madrid High Court annulled his appointment because Malaysia had not been properly notified. Stampa moved the case to Paris, and in February 2022 he ordered Malaysia to pay $14.92 billion. The heirs then tried to seize Malaysian assets in France, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, and failed. In Spain, Stampa was convicted of contempt of court, the offence of defying a court's order. He was sentenced to six months in prison and barred from acting as an arbitrator for a year, and the Madrid Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in May 2024.

The French courts dismantled the award in stages. The Paris Court of Appeal held in July 2023 that the arbitrator had no power over the dispute. On 6 November 2024 France's highest court, the Cour de Cassation, dismissed the heirs' appeal because the clause named an official who no longer exists. In December 2025 Malaysia announced that the Paris Court of Appeal had annulled the whole award, because no valid arbitration agreement bound Malaysia, and had ordered the claimants to pay 200,000 euros in costs. The sultanate's secretary-general said the legal fight was not over.

Malaysia treats the claim as an attack on its sovereignty and does not accept any claim to Sabah. The heirs had asked only for money, and even a full win would not have moved the border. The case shows how far an old paper can travel in modern courts. A colonial-era deed can produce a real multibillion-dollar award, and that award still has to be enforced against a state in courts that will ask whether the state ever consented.

swazi-concessions.story:
Eswatini, called Swaziland until 2018, is a small kingdom in southern Africa between what is now South Africa and Mozambique. Mbandzeni was its king from 1875 until he died in 1889. He had been chosen as a motherless boy, after the king-designate Ludvonga died in 1874. He inherited a strong army of more than 15,000 men and a practice of giving land rights to outsiders, since his father Mswati II had already granted land to Boers, Dutch-descended settlers, in the 1850s.

A concession is a grant of a right by a ruler, such as the right to graze cattle on a stretch of land, mine it, trade there or collect a fee. In Mbandzeni's time such papers became the way Swaziland was carved up. Concession seekers from Britain and from the Transvaal, the Boer republic next door, crowded into his capital at Mbekelweni, and the discovery of gold in the Transvaal brought more of them. The king and his officials were paid in gold, cattle or goods. 'Offy' Shepstone, a nephew of Sir Theophilus Shepstone, the administrator of the Natal colony, advised him, and more grants followed. Many of them overlapped, so that two people might hold rights to the same thing.

By one account, Boers tricked the king, who could not read or write, by having him mark papers with a cross after telling him the land concessions were not permanent, though the papers said they were. A ruler who cannot read the document is at the mercy of whoever explains it to him.

Mbandzeni tried to protect himself through alliances. In 1879 he sent about 10,000 soldiers to help the British defeat Sekhukhune, the Pedi king, and kept Zulu raids out of the Transvaal. Britain rewarded this by recognising Swaziland's independence and promising protection against Zulu and Boer encroachment. The concessions undid that promise. They gave the Boers and British a stake inside the country, and these interests were used at the conventions of 1884 and 1894, agreements between outside powers. No Swazi represented the kingdom directly at either negotiation. Shepstone spoke for Swazi interests in 1884 and Allister Miller in 1894. The border they drew with the South African Republic cut off many Swazi homes, including royal villages, which is why many Swazi people live in South Africa's Mpumalanga province today. The 1894 convention later made Swaziland a protectorate of that republic, meaning that it took charge of Swaziland's outside affairs.

Mbandzeni is quoted as saying on his deathbed that the Swazi kingship would die with him. A regency followed under Queen Tibati Nkambule until his young son took the throne.

This entry belongs with purchases of territory because no single sale took place. Rights over the country passed in many small private grants, each of which looked like a limited business deal. Once enough foreign holders existed, their governments had a reason to step in, and sovereignty was settled above the king's head.

tiran-sanafir.story:
Tiran and Sanafir are two uninhabited islands in the Red Sea at the entrance to the Gulf of Aqaba. Tiran covers about 80 square kilometres and is a popular place for divers. Its value is its position. It controls the narrow shipping lane that leads to Eilat in Israel and Aqaba in Jordan, and that lane is Israel's only way from the gulf to the Red Sea. Egypt closed it on 22 May 1967, and the closure was among the main causes of the Arab-Israeli war that year.

Who the islands belong to has long been argued. In 1949 and 1950, after Israeli forces reached the gulf, Egypt put troops on them with Saudi agreement, because Saudi Arabia had no navy to protect them. In 1954 Egypt told the UN Security Council that they had been sovereign Egyptian territory since a 1906 frontier deal with the Ottoman Empire. In 1957 Saudi Arabia asserted its own sovereignty in a memorandum to the UN. Israel captured the islands in 1967 and gave them back to Egypt under the 1979 peace treaty. Egyptian lawmakers said in 2017 that Saudi Arabia had asked for them back in 1984, 1989 and 1990.

In April 2016, during a visit to Cairo by the Saudi king, Egypt announced that it would hand them over. The Egyptian government said that the islands had always been Saudi and were only under Egyptian care. Critics linked the deal to billions of dollars of Saudi aid to President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's government and called it a sell-off of national land. The announcement set off the largest anti-government protests since he took office in 2014, and hundreds of people were arrested, most of whom were later released. Israel was told in writing weeks before the public announcement and gave its approval, because the change touched the military annex of its peace treaty with Egypt. Saudi Arabia said it would honour that treaty's terms for the islands.

The fight then moved through Egypt's institutions. In January 2017 the Supreme Administrative Court ruled against the transfer, and the lawyer Khalid Ali obtained court papers supporting Egyptian sovereignty. In April the Urgent Affairs Court set that ruling aside. The head of parliament, Ali Abdel Aal, said parliament would not recognise any ruling on the agreement. Supporters argued that ratifying treaties is parliament's right. On 13 June police beat several dozen protesters in downtown Cairo, and on 14 June parliament approved the deal by a vote in which supporters were asked to stand. A week later the Constitutional Court halted all rulings in the case, and Sisi ratified the treaty on 24 June. A government report said the agreement ended Egyptian sovereignty while Egypt kept administering the area for now, for the security of both countries.

Whether this counts as a sale depends on who is describing it, since no price is stated in the treaty and aid is only what critics connect it to. It shows two things about moving territory today. A transfer between states can involve a third country whose treaties depend on the old arrangement. A government's own courts may object, and the outcome then depends on which institution has the last word.

tompkins-patagonia.story:
Patagonia is the thinly settled southern end of South America, shared by Chile and Argentina. Douglas Tompkins was an American who loved it from a six-month climbing expedition there in 1968. He had founded the outdoor company The North Face, which he sold after a few years, and then the fashion company Esprit with his first wife. In 1990 he retired from business and moved to southern Chile.

He wanted to do what wealthy Americans had long done at home, which is to buy wild land and protect it. He started buying parcels in Chaitén province through go-betweens, so that sellers and neighbours would not notice and prices would not climb. In 1994 he announced Pumalín Park, 275,000 hectares, larger than England's biggest national park.

The trouble came from the park's shape. It ran from the Pacific Ocean to the Argentine border, which in effect cut Chile in two. Chile had just left a long military dictatorship, during which it had nearly gone to war with Argentina over the location of this frontier, and many people did not welcome a foreigner buying land on this scale. Parliament debated whether he was undermining national sovereignty. The military and Patagonian senators asked whether the park threatened the country's unity and would block roads and power lines. Small farmers without land titles said he ignored their rights.

In 1996 he reached an agreement with President Frei to stop buying land and to allow infrastructure across it. Both sides later cancelled that agreement, and he more than doubled his Chilean holdings and bought more in Argentina, until he had spent about three decades acquiring more than a million hectares. He promised to give it all to the state, but distrust between him and the government limited his donations before he died in a kayaking accident in December 2015. His widow, Kristine McDivitt Tompkins, a former head of the Patagonia clothing company, pledged more than one million acres to Chile in March 2017. In January 2018 President Michelle Bachelet announced decrees creating national parks from the land, including Pumalín and Patagonia.

This case belongs here because it marks the outer limit of what money buys. Tompkins held the largest network of privately owned nature reserves in the world, and he still held only ownership. Chilean and Argentine law applied on every hectare, and the governments kept their police, courts and power to build roads. Even so, one foreign owner's control of a strip from the sea to the border was treated as a question of national territory, and the political fight was about that. The question was finally closed when the family gave the land to the state.

transylvania-purchase.story:
Before the American Revolution, the land west of the Appalachian Mountains was contested by several groups at once. The Royal Proclamation of 1763, issued by the British Crown after the French and Indian War, declared that land Indian Territory and forbade colonial settlement there. Settlers, traders and trappers kept going anyway. In the 1768 Treaty of Fort Stanwix, the Haudenosaunee, who claimed much of what is now Kentucky without living there, gave up their claim to Britain. The Shawnee and Cherokee, who actually used the land, were not consulted. The Shawnee fought Virginia in Lord Dunmore's War in 1774, lost, and gave up their claims south of the Ohio River. Virginia and North Carolina both also claimed parts of the area.

Into this came Richard Henderson, a North Carolina judge and land speculator. His Transylvania Company had a simple idea. If it bought the land directly from the Cherokee, it could perhaps get around the proclamation and win approval as a colony owned by its proprietors, as some early British colonies had been. Investors would profit by reselling land to settlers.

In 1775, at Sycamore Shoals, most leading Cherokee chiefs accepted a treaty selling a huge tract covering central and western Kentucky and part of north central Tennessee. The price was goods that some scholars estimate at about £10,000. Henderson hired the frontiersman Daniel Boone to cut the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap so that buyers could get there. In May 1775 settlers agreed a written compact of government, a plan for running their own affairs.

Then the Revolutionary War began, and most settlement stopped except around the established towns. It also brought new governments that had every reason to reject him. The Virginia General Assembly cancelled the Kentucky claim in 1778 and North Carolina cancelled the Tennessee part in 1783. Neither left him empty-handed. Each gave Henderson and his partners a grant of 200,000 acres, and Henderson, Kentucky, stands on the land he received along the Ohio River.

The legal lesson is about who gets to recognise a purchase. Henderson's deed came from people who lived on and used the land, yet the colonial governments applied their own rule, under which they alone could approve such a purchase, and they had claims of their own. So the deal gave him no title they would accept. The colony is described as extra-legal, meaning that it stood outside any law, and it existed only until someone with a government could rule on it. Its one lasting result was the compensation grant, which came from those same governments.

trump-gaza.story:
Gaza is a small Palestinian coastal territory on the Mediterranean, devastated by war by early 2025. Hamas, a Palestinian armed group, had ruled it. On 9 February 2025, flying to the Super Bowl in New Orleans on Air Force One, US President Donald Trump told reporters, "I'm committed to buying and owning Gaza." He said other Middle Eastern states might rebuild sections of it under American auspices, and that the United States would make sure Hamas did not move back. He called the place "a demolition site" and had also spoken of permanently moving Palestinians out to create a "Riviera of the Middle East".

The remarks named no seller and no price. A purchase needs someone with the power to hand over the land and a sum agreed with them, and neither was described. Ezzat El Rashq of the Hamas political bureau answered that "Gaza is not a property to be sold and bought", called it part of occupied Palestinian land, and said that Palestinians would defeat any displacement plans.

Nothing was bought. The entry is here as a statement by a head of state that uses the language of a land deal for a place with a resident population and no party offering it for sale.

tulagi-lease.story:
Tulagi is a small island in the Solomon Islands, a Pacific country east of Papua New Guinea. It covers about two square kilometres, has 1,200 people, and has a deep-water harbour of the kind navies want. The Solomon Islands has a national government and also provincial governments, and Tulagi falls within Central Province. That division of power decided the case.

In September 2019 the Solomon Islands cut its ties with Taiwan and opened diplomatic relations with China. The next day, 22 September, the Central Province premier, Stanley Manetiva, signed a strategic cooperation agreement with China Sam Enterprise Group, a Chinese state-linked developer. It gave the company exclusive development rights to Tulagi and its neighbouring islands, and RNZ, New Zealand's public broadcaster, described it as a five-year lease deal. The text spoke vaguely of trade, minerals, possible oil and gas, and a special economic zone, an area with its own business rules.

When local media reported the deal, residents, national officials and Western diplomats were alarmed. One senior diplomat said the wording could allow strategic assets such as deep-sea ports, which would give China a foothold in the region.

In October the national Attorney-General, John Muria, the government's chief lawyer, declared it unlawful and unenforceable and said it must be terminated at once. There were several reasons. It had not been reviewed by his office, as the law required. The province did not have the power to negotiate such an agreement. China Sam did not hold foreign investor status, and an illegal clause tried to exempt it from the foreign-investor rules. The prime minister's office, under Manasseh Sogavare, repeated the same conclusion. The premier then said the deal was not legally binding and was no longer an issue.

Anyone trying to lease a whole island meets the same question here. A signature is only as good as the signer's authority. A local government may be willing, and may even be eager, while the national government holds the power over foreign investment and treaties and can cancel the agreement with one letter, as happened within about a month.

white-rajahs-sarawak.story:
Sarawak is a territory on the north-west coast of Borneo, today a state of Malaysia. For 105 years it was ruled by a British family, the Brookes, who held the title of Rajah, a word for a king or prince. It is one of the few cases on record of a private person from abroad gaining a territory and ruling it as a monarch.

Before 1841 Sarawak was part of the realm of the Sultanate of Brunei, and owed loyalty to the sultan. James Brooke, a man of British origin born in India in 1803, helped the sultan's side fight piracy and uprisings among the local peoples. In 1841 Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II granted him the area around the town of Sarawak, now Kuching, and the nearby Bau mining district. No price was paid. He was later confirmed with the title of Rajah.

Brooke rebuilt the government on the British model. He and his successor leased or annexed more land from Brunei until the state covered much of northern Borneo. James's will set the succession along the male line. His nephew Charles ruled from 1868 to 1917, and Charles's son Vyner from 1917 to 1946. In 1941, just before the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, Vyner ended the Rajah's absolute rule by giving new powers to the Council Negri, the local parliament.

After the Japanese occupation, Vyner ceded Sarawak to Britain's Colonial Office in 1946. Cession means a formal handing-over of territory. It was contested from the start. His nephew and legal heir, Anthony Brooke, objected, and so did most native members of the Council Negri. Because it was unclear whether the cession was legal, Britain also passed an annexation bill. An anti-cession movement grew, and the British governor Duncan Stewart was assassinated by members of a group seeking union with Indonesia. Sarawak became a British Crown colony, and in 1963 it became a state of Malaysia under the Malaysia Agreement.

The family's grant shows what such a position rested on. Brooke's title came from a ruler who had the power to give it and who owed him a favour, in a place where no stronger outside power objected. Sources describe Sarawak as a sovereign state under the Brookes, though how other states formally treated it is not known. The rule lasted as long as outside powers accepted it, and it ended when one family member signed it away over the objection of his heir and of the local parliament.

arctic-sanctuary-greenpeace-flag.story:
The middle of the Arctic Ocean, around the North Pole, lies beyond the national zones of the five countries with Arctic coasts. No state rules those waters. The Arctic sanctuary is a proposal to protect that area from oil drilling and mining, promoted above all by the environmental group Greenpeace. It would work something like a nature reserve in international waters. As of 2016, only 4.7 percent of the Arctic marine area was protected.

Campaigners face a basic problem. A national government can create a park on its own territory by passing a law, but no single country has the power to do so for waters that belong to no country. There were also no international rules at the time for creating marine protected areas beyond national control, so an Arctic sanctuary would have needed new agreements between states.

In April 2013 four young people working with Greenpeace, led by two young Indigenous people from the Arctic, trekked to the Pole. Their trip coincided with a meeting of the Arctic Council's senior officials at the Barneo ice camp, a temporary base on the sea ice. They cut a hole in the ice and lowered a flag designed by a child from Malaysia to the seabed about four kilometres down, at the spot where a Russian submarine had placed a flag in 2007. The flag was attached to a glass and titanium capsule holding the signatures of nearly three million people. Josefina Skerk, 26, a member of the Saami parliament in Sweden, said the area "belongs to no person or nation" and should be declared a global sanctuary, closed to oil companies and political posturing.

The flag was a piece of protest and made no claim. Its point was to answer the Russian flag with one standing for everyone. Neither flag had any legal effect on who may use the seabed.

Governments have taken up the idea in words. In 2008 the European Parliament raised the possibility of a treaty modelled on the Antarctic Treaty, and in a 2014 resolution it called for a sanctuary in the waters outside coastal states' zones. Such resolutions do not bind anyone. No sanctuary has been created, and it remains a campaign aim.

arktika-2007-flag.story:
The seabed under the North Pole is at the centre of a legal question about who may one day have rights to what lies under the Arctic Ocean. Under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal state controls the resources in a zone reaching 200 nautical miles (about 370 km) from its shore, and it can seek rights over seabed beyond that if it shows by scientific evidence that the seabed is a natural extension of its land. Lindsay Parson of Britain's National Oceanography Centre explained that the 200-mile zones of the five Arctic coastal states leave a central area of about 300,000 to 400,000 square kilometres in question. Russia first submitted its claim to part of that seabed in 2001. As Arctic ice shrinks, the area has become easier to reach.

Arktika 2007 was the expedition that went to gather evidence. The research ship Akademik Fedorov left Saint Petersburg on 10 July 2007 with about 100 scientists and two small Mir submarines, and the nuclear icebreaker Rossiya led it through the ice. The scientists wanted to find out whether undersea ridges such as the Lomonosov Ridge are linked to the Siberian shelf. Early in the trip the Fedorov's propeller motor failed in the Barents Sea, and the crew fixed it within hours while the icebreaker turned back to help. After test dives north of Franz Josef Land, the expedition reached the Pole.

In August the two submarines went down to the seabed, a depth of 4,261 metres. This was the first crewed descent to the ocean floor at the Pole. Artur Chilingarov, the expedition's leader and a member of parliament, was on board along with the pilots Anatoly Sagalevich and Yevgeny Chernyaev. They collected specimens and left a rust-proof titanium flag. Chilingarov said people could find it in a thousand years. All three were later named Heroes of the Russian Federation.

Other governments answered quickly. Canada's foreign minister, Peter MacKay, said this was not the 15th century, when countries could plant flags and claim territory. A US State Department spokesman said the flag had no legal standing. Parson called the dive a scientific achievement that meant very little as a legal claim.

The legal reason is the one that matters to anyone hoping to claim part of the world by arriving first. Under the Law of the Sea treaty the seabed past national zones cannot be taken by occupation or by planting a symbol. A country wanting more has to build a scientific case and submit it under the treaty process. Flag-planting does not enter into it. The flag, set there by a large state with an icebreaker, changed nothing about who owns what, and it remains a symbol.

eastern-greenland-case.mechanism: Light use of remote land can still be enough for a state to own it, if that state has shown authority there. A later proclamation and a few private stations did not displace Denmark, and a foreign minister's spoken promise counted against Norway.
eastern-greenland-case.story:
Greenland's far east coast is one of the emptiest places on Earth. It once had an Inuit population, but the last person was seen in 1823. By 1931 the stretch that this case concerns had no permanent population except for hunters and trappers at three main Norwegian stations, Jonsbu, Myggbukta and Antarctic Havn, and some smaller ones. Today it lies in Northeast Greenland National Park.

Norway and Denmark had shared this history. The medieval Norse colony in Greenland recognised the King of Norway, and Denmark and Norway were one kingdom from 1537 to 1814. When they separated, Denmark kept Greenland.

In June 1931 Hallvard Devold, a founder of the Norwegian Arctic Trading Company, raised the Norwegian flag at Myggbukta. On 10 July Norway issued a royal proclamation occupying the area and named it Erik the Red's Land, after the founder of the first Norse settlements in Greenland. Its legal theory was that this part of Greenland was terra nullius, Latin for land belonging to no one. Under old rules, a state can claim such land by actually occupying it. Norway argued that Denmark had never effectively done so.

Denmark went to the Permanent Court of International Justice, the world court of the time, two days later. It asked the court to declare the occupation unlawful and invalid. The case also turned on an earlier conversation. In July 1919 Norway's foreign minister, Nils Ihlen, told the Danish minister that Norway would not make difficulties over Denmark's claim to all of Greenland, and Denmark treated that as binding.

On 5 April 1933 the court ruled for Denmark by twelve votes to two and found the proclamation unlawful and invalid. Norway then gave up the claim.

The ruling teaches two rules that matter to anyone hoping to claim empty land. First, the amount of activity needed to hold a territory depends on the place. In a frozen, unpopulated region, a state can own it with little presence, as long as it has shown that it means to rule and has acted accordingly. So a settler who finds a coast with no government on it cannot assume it is free. Second, a foreign minister's spoken statement can bind a state. Private stations and a later flag could not outweigh Denmark's prior authority.

hans-island.story:
Hans Island, called Tartupaluk in Greenlandic, is a bare, uninhabited rock of 1.3 square kilometres in Nares Strait, the narrow sea between Canada's Ellesmere Island and Greenland. Greenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark, so the dispute over it was between Canada and Denmark. It is a useful case because it shows how two friendly states handled a small rock that neither would give up.

In 1973 the two countries signed a treaty fixing their sea boundary through the strait, and the line deliberately stopped either side of the island because they could not agree who owned it. Canada said the island came with the 1880 transfer of the Hudson's Bay Company's lands to Canada. Denmark said it was part of Greenland and had been used by Greenlandic Inuit for hunting, and pointed to an expedition with Danish participation that named it in 1853, and to its geology. Neither side took the question to an international court.

What followed became known as the Whisky War. Visitors from each side left flags and bottles of drink for the other. In 2005 Canada's defence minister raised a flag there and Denmark sent a warship, and NPR reported a summer of flag-planting and gift-leaving. No one was hurt, and the two countries are NATO allies.

On 14 June 2022 the foreign ministers Mélanie Joly of Canada and Jeppe Kofod of Denmark, with Greenland's premier Múte Egede, settled it. The agreement split the island along a natural ridge, roughly 60 percent to Denmark and the rest to Canada. This gave the two countries their first land border. It also settled their remaining sea boundary in the Lincoln and Labrador seas. The ministers exchanged bottles of Canadian Sortilège whisky and Danish Gammel Dansk bitter.

Nobody from outside could have stepped in and claimed the rock during those 49 years. Being disputed did not make it free, since both states already claimed it. The case shows the reverse of the micronation idea, in which a gap between claims creates an opening. Here the gap closed by agreement between the two states.

svalbard-treaty.story:
Svalbard is a group of Arctic islands north of mainland Norway, about twice the size of Belgium. It has about 2,500 residents and no Indigenous people. It is often cited by people interested in places outside normal national rules, so it helps to know exactly how it works.

Until the 20th century Svalbard was terra nullius, land belonging to no state. Whalers came first and then miners from many countries, and they worked with almost no law. Once coal mining grew, disputes between miners and owners had no court to go to, and that created demand for someone to govern.

The answer was a treaty, signed in Paris on 9 February 1920 and in force from 14 August 1925. It recognises Norway's full and unqualified sovereignty, meaning supreme legal authority, over the islands. In exchange Norway accepted limits. Citizens and companies of every treaty country may live there and have equal rights to fish, hunt, mine and run businesses. Norway may collect only enough tax to pay for running Svalbard, so its budget is kept apart from the mainland's, and not all Norwegian law applies. Article 9 bans naval bases and fortifications, which restricts military use though the islands are not fully demilitarised. The whole archipelago is a visa-free zone under the treaty.

Russia uses its rights through its coal settlements at Barentsburg and Pyramiden. The treaty began with 14 parties and had 49 by 2026.

People sometimes describe Svalbard as a place belonging to no one where anyone can move. That is a misunderstanding. No visa is needed to enter, but Norway governs it, and a resident must obey Norwegian rules as they apply there. The treaty guarantees the right to come and do business, and it gives no right to rule anything.

The case shows the most workable form of unowned land being settled. Land with no government attracted people, the people's disputes created a demand for law, and the outside powers solved this by handing the land to one state on conditions. Nobody got an independent territory. A group wanting one today would find that the same process, if it happened, would most likely end with a government in charge.

t3-ice-island-escamilla.story:
T-3, also called Fletcher's Ice Island, was a huge slab of glacial ice in the Arctic Ocean, about 11 by 5 kilometres and roughly 99 percent ice. It moved slowly around the ocean with the currents. An American first sighted it in 1947, and from 1952 the US Air Force and Navy used it as a research platform, under Colonel Joseph O. Fletcher, because it was so steady. It had huts, a power plant and an airstrip, and it held a permanent station from October 1962, usually with 25 to 30 staff. The only authority on site was a station manager, chosen by the Naval Arctic Research Laboratory.

On 16 July 1970 an argument broke out over some home-made raisin wine. Mario Escamilla, the wine's owner, was told that a co-worker, Donald Leavitt, had taken it. Escamilla borrowed a rifle and went back to his trailer to confront him. The station manager, Bennie Lightsey, stopped him and tried to take the rifle, and in the struggle Lightsey was shot and killed. There were 19 people on the team then, and now they had a killing with no police or court, on a piece of ice that belonged to no one.

Both men were Americans, but that does not by itself let a US court try a crime abroad. Federal crimes need a legal hook, called jurisdiction, meaning a court's authority over a place or event. The ice then lay inside the Arctic sector Canada had claimed, but Canada chose not to act. American officials flew Escamilla to Dulles Airport in Virginia and charged him under the special law for crimes at sea, arguing that the ice was on the high seas, the open ocean outside every country's waters.

A jury convicted him of involuntary manslaughter and he received three years. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, heard the case with six judges and split evenly on whether US law reached an unclaimed ice island. An even split leaves the trial court's ruling in place, so the case stayed in American courts without any rule being set. The judges did find other errors in the trial and ordered a new one, at which he was acquitted. Congress settled the question only in 1984, by changing federal law.

The station was abandoned in 1978 and the ice drifted on. The case shows what happens when something odd is neither land nor a ship. Living beyond clear national law did not remove anyone's government. It left people with no local police, and when something went wrong, the country that supplied the station stepped in and argued about the legal reasons afterwards.

wrangel-island-expedition.story:
Wrangel Island lies in the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia, across the Chukchi Sea from Alaska, and in 1921 nobody lived on it. It had already killed people. In 1914 survivors of the ship Karluk, crushed in the ice during an expedition organised by the Arctic explorer Vilhjalmur Stefansson, were stranded there for nine months until their captain walked across the sea to Siberia for help.

Stefansson believed the island could be claimed by simply occupying it. Russia had declared it Russian in 1916, but in 1921 he sent five people on a speculative attempt to claim it for Canada, saying he wanted to head off a Japanese claim. They were the Canadian Allan Crawford and the Americans Fred Maurer, Lorne Knight and Milton Galle, and Ada Blackjack, an Iñupiaq woman of about 23 from Nome, Alaska. She had been abandoned by her husband, cleaned houses and sewed for miners, and could not afford to care for her son. She took the job as seamstress and cook, sewing the fur clothing, in order to earn money for him.

A relief ship, the Teddy Bear, stuck in the ice in 1922 and turned back. Food ran short. In January 1923 Crawford, Maurer and Galle set out across the frozen sea toward Siberia to get help and were never seen again. Knight, too sick to go, died of scurvy that June. Blackjack, left alone, kept herself alive for eight months in all, until a ship rescued her in August 1923.

The same ship left a new party of 13, the American Charles Wells and 12 Inuit. In 1924 the Soviet Union sent the ship Krasny Oktyabr, or Red October, and took them away, by then 14 people after a birth on the island. Wells died of pneumonia in Vladivostok, two children died, and the survivors got home with money raised by the American Red Cross.

The island remains Russian and became a World Heritage Site in 2004. The episode shows the two ways a small private colony fails. The first is supply, because a single missed ship can mean death. The second is that an occupation without a government's backing has no protection, since the nearest state can end it by sending one vessel.

deepsea-ventures-claim.story:
Far out on the deep Pacific floor lie manganese nodules, potato-sized lumps containing copper, nickel, cobalt and manganese. They sit thousands of metres down, well beyond any country's waters. By the 1970s companies believed they might one day be worth mining. The law had almost nothing to say about them. The ocean floor had seen little commercial use apart from undersea cables, and the Law of the Sea treaty, the main international agreement on use of the oceans, was still being negotiated. In June 1974 the billionaire Howard Hughes's ship, Hughes Glomar Explorer, sailed from Long Beach, reportedly to mine nodules.

Deepsea Ventures Inc. of Gloucester Point, Virginia, decided to try to establish a right before anyone wrote the rules. On 15 November 1974 its president, John Flipse, sent Secretary of State Henry Kissinger a "Notice of Discovery and Claim of Exclusive Mining Rights, and Request for Diplomatic Protection and Protection of Investment". He also recorded a copy at the Gloucester County Circuit Court, an ordinary local court where property papers are filed. Copies went by registered mail to cabinet members, congressional committees, ambassadors of maritime countries, oceanographers and other companies. The idea was publicity. The older rule for unowned things is that whoever finds and takes them first has a claim, and the company wanted everyone to be on notice that it had found this deposit first.

The tract covered 60,000 square kilometres of the northeastern Pacific. The company promised commercial production within 15 years, running for 40 years. It claimed exclusive rights to mine and sell the nodules, and it took care to say that it was claiming no territory and was not asking the United States to do so. That distinction reflects the rule that nobody could own the high seas. It wanted a right to the minerals, in the way someone may have a right to fish from a sea no one owns. The magazine Reason called it the world's first ocean mining claim and argued that the minerals were unclaimed property for whoever made the effort.

The legal ground then shifted. The 1982 treaty put the seabed outside national zones under an international authority and declared that no one may own it by claiming it. Mining is not known to have taken place under the claim, and no court is known to have ruled on it. The case is the clearest early try at a private claim outside any country, and it shows why such a claim needed a government's protection, which is what Flipse asked Kissinger for.

international-seabed-authority.story:
About half of the world's ocean area lies over seabed that belongs to no country. Its floor holds metal-rich nodules and other mineral deposits. The 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea calls this seabed the common heritage of all mankind, and it sets up an international body to run it, the International Seabed Authority. The authority is based in Kingston, Jamaica, and held its first meeting there on 16 November 1994, the day the treaty took effect. It has 172 members, 171 countries and the European Union, and is funded by members and mining contractors. The United States has not ratified the treaty and is not a member.

It works differently from a land claim. Nobody can own this seabed by finding or occupying it. A company that wants to mine there needs two things, a contract with the authority and the backing of a member country, called a sponsor. The sponsor answers for the company's conduct. So a small country can sponsor a company, as Nauru and Tonga have, and it is the country that gives the company its way in.

The authority has two jobs that pull against each other. It authorises mining and it is also supposed to protect the seabed environment. Since 1994 it has approved more than two dozen exploration contracts in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, most of them in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico, where nodules contain copper, cobalt and other metals used in batteries. It has not approved any commercial mining. It is still writing the rules, while scientists and environmental groups warn of harm to the ocean and call for a pause.

The politics sharpened in 2026. The council met in March without finishing the mining rules, leaving benefit-sharing, liability and environmental compensation unresolved. The authority opened an inquiry into whether two contractors, NORI and TOML, had broken their obligations by seeking American mining permits. On 18 July 2026 a specialist chamber of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea ordered the authority to respect due process, meaning fair procedure, in that inquiry. Two days later the council extended NORI's exploration contract to 2031.

For anyone thinking of founding something on the seabed, the rule is plain. Under this treaty the bottom of the sea past national zones cannot be taken, and the only legal route to its minerals is a contract through this body. Countries outside the treaty, such as the United States, are the main open question.

metals-company.story:
The Metals Company is a Canadian-founded business that wants to mine metal-rich nodules from the Pacific floor. It began as DeepGreen Metals in 2011. The nodules, which contain nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese, lie in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, about 1,500 miles southwest of San Diego, on seabed that no country owns. Under the Law of the Sea treaty, that seabed is controlled by the International Seabed Authority, and a company needs a contract with the authority and a sponsoring member country.

The company worked within that system by using small Pacific states. Its subsidiary NORI held an exploration contract sponsored by Nauru, and it later bought TOML, sponsored by Tonga. In 2012 DeepGreen agreed to sell 50 percent of its future nickel and copper from the NORI area to the commodity trader Glencore. In 2021 it merged with a listed shell company, a firm with a stock listing and no business, in a $2.9 billion deal, and took its current name.

In June 2021 Nauru told the authority that it intended to begin mining. A rule in the treaty system meant that this started a two-year deadline to finish the mining rules. The deadline passed and the rules were not finished, which left the company with exploration rights and no way to mine.

It then turned to another route. The United States never joined the treaty, and it has its own older law on seabed mining. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the American ocean agency, to speed up permits under that law. Four days later the company's American arm applied. NOAA published its application for public comment in August 2026, and no permit had been issued by that month.

The authority responded by opening an inquiry into whether NORI and TOML had broken their contracts. The two companies took it to a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal in June 2026, and on 18 July the chamber ordered the authority to respect fair procedure, without suspending the inquiry. The main case is undecided. NORI's contract was extended to 2031, and TOML's runs to January 2027 with an extension pending.

The company stands on both sides of the question. Its subsidiaries hold contracts under the treaty, and its American arm seeks a permit that would bypass that treaty. What remains open is whether one country's permit can give a company a right to mine an area that most of the world has agreed to manage together. The answer will affect anyone hoping to operate outside the shared system with one government's approval.

bitnation.story:
A government keeps registers. It records who you are, who you married, when your child was born and what you own, and other institutions accept those records because a government stands behind them. Bitnation asked what would happen if ordinary people could keep such records themselves on a blockchain, a shared public ledger that many computers maintain together and that no single office controls. It called itself a voluntary nation, because all its citizens chose to join.

Susanne Tarkowski Tempelhof founded it on 14 July 2014. She grew up in a Franco-Swedish family in which her father had been stateless for a decade, and she told a Vice writer that Antarctica was the only place in the world not covered by a state's rule. Bitnation had no territory. Joining meant recording your identity and vital events through a program on the Ethereum blockchain.

In 2015 it released software for blockchain ID cards and launched a Refugee Emergency Response project that offered ID records and Bitcoin debit cards to refugees reaching Europe without papers. From December 2015 it offered a blockchain notary service to e-residents of Estonia, foreigners who hold a digital identity from that country. In 2017 it launched Pangea, a system for settling disputes by private arbitration, with a proposed token of its own. Its refugee ID won a UNESCO prize. Tempelhof told IBTimes that she hoped Bitnation would be recognised as a sovereign entity, which would set a precedent for open software counting as a jurisdiction, an area of legal authority.

The Vice writer who joined in 2016 found about 25 volunteer embassies, including a German castle run as a bed and breakfast, and reported limited services and little interest. The gap between the record and its use showed up at the moment that mattered. A marriage on a blockchain is real data, but a tax office or a hospital has no duty to honour it. A refugee ID is a useful piece of evidence, but a border guard or an asylum officer is not bound by it. Because no state recognised Bitnation, an embassy could do little for an asylum seeker.

By August 2022 its web domain had been sold, and the project is considered defunct. It remains a test of the idea that record-keeping is the core of a state. The records worked as a technical matter, but no government or institution had a duty to act on them.

citydao.story:
A DAO, or decentralised autonomous organisation, is a group that makes decisions and holds money through software on a blockchain, a shared public ledger. Until 2021 no US law said clearly how such a group could own anything. That July, a new Wyoming law took effect that let a DAO register as a kind of company, a limited liability company, and so hold property in its own name. Wyoming was the only state then offering this.

Scott Fitsimones started the idea with a tweet just after the law took effect, asking whether a DAO could buy physical land. The answer was CityDAO, formed under that law with the mission of building "a city of the future" with everything recorded on the blockchain. In October 2021 the group bought 40 acres west of Clark, about 30 minutes from Cody, for around $100,000. Members call it Parcel 0.

Day to day it works like an online club that owns a field. Members hold a digital token called a Citizenship NFT, which lets them vote on proposals, visit the land and suggest uses for it. Citizen here means only someone who holds the token. It gives no legal citizenship, no passport and no exemption. Fitsimones described the land as an experiment in how a DAO might govern what happens on it.

In June 2022 CityDAO told a Wyoming legislative committee that it had about 6,500 citizens. It said future work might include buying more property and trying to incorporate an actual city, if counties agreed, with deeds, titles and tax records on the blockchain. A town in the United States exists under state law, so this plan meant working within that law.

In May 2023 the local press reported that the land remained undeveloped, with a well and a flat building area, and that zoning rules, the local limits on how land may be used, may allow only one house on each 40-acre lot. So the ordinary county rules applied to the group just as they would to a rancher. What has since become of the project is not known.

CityDAO never claimed independence. It shows what a blockchain community can actually do. It can pool money across the world and own land through a state-chartered company, and every member stays subject to that state's law.

decentraland-land.story:
Decentraland is an online 3D world, reached through a web browser, in which people buy plots of virtual land, build on them and walk around as cartoon figures called avatars. The Argentine developers Ari Meilich and Esteban Ordano began it in 2015. It is included because its plots are sold and spoken of as land, and it has its own currency and a form of self-rule.

A plot is a token, a unique digital ownership record on the Ethereum blockchain, a shared public ledger, and it is paid for in the world's currency, MANA. The company raised $26 million by selling MANA coins in 2017, when each coin cost two cents. The world opened to the public in February 2020 and is overseen by the nonprofit Decentraland Foundation, with users voting on policy.

The first map, Genesis City, has 90,601 plots, which sold for about $20 each at launch. There can be only that many, so scarcity is written into the code. During the 2021 cryptocurrency boom, plots sold for $6,000 to $100,000, and in November a virtual real-estate company paid $2.43 million for one. Use stayed small. The analytics firm DappRadar counted fewer than 1,000 users a day making transactions in October 2022, and as few as 38 on one day, while Decentraland claimed 8,000 daily users. Reviewers criticised its bugs and its mostly empty world.

Self-rule has limits of its own. In November 2021 a community vote on banning the name Hitler for avatars failed to get enough votes to take effect.

What a buyer gets is a record that says this token controls this square in this program. It carries no rights under any country's land law. There are no deeds in a county office and no police, and the plot exists only as long as the software keeps running. The buyer stays a resident and taxpayer of a real country. Decentraland remains open. Barbados announced an embassy there in 2021, using the language of territory for a place that has none of its legal effects.

dominion-of-melchizedek.story:
The Dominion of Melchizedek calls itself a sovereign country, meaning that it answers to no other government. It has no confirmed population and no land it actually controls. The US Securities and Exchange Commission has described it as non-existent, and the EU lists its documents among fantasy passports. It appears here because it shows how the claim of statehood can be used as a tool for fraud.

The American Mark Pedley declared it in 1990, possibly with his father David, who had been convicted of financial crimes in the 1970s. Mark had his own convictions, including a $6 million currency fraud in 1986, and his parole was revoked in 1991 for promoting a fictitious country. He used other names, including Branch Vinedresser. The name comes from the biblical king and priest Melchizedek.

It moved from claim to claim. It first claimed Malpelo, a Colombian island 300 miles off the Pacific coast. It then announced Karitane Shoal in the South Pacific, which appears to have been invented, and which a spokesman described as 14 square miles of sandy beaches. It also claimed French-owned Clipperton Island, Bokak Atoll in the Marshall Islands, and Marie Byrd Land, a part of Antarctica no state claims. Its people were banned from the Fijian island of Rotuma after working with dissidents seeking to secede. Nobody had to live on any of these places, because what it sold was the claim of statehood.

The business worked like this. A "country" can claim to issue bank licences, and a bank licence can be used to open what looks like a real financial institution elsewhere. About 300 licences were claimed to have been sold by the end of the 1990s. In 1991 shell banks in Washington, D.C., tried to get loans using fake Melchizedek securities and were shut down. One investment scheme took over $4 million from at least 1,400 people. Passports sold for up to $3,500, and three people posing as officials were arrested in the Philippines in 1998 in a scheme that took about $1 million. One source estimates the total raised at over $500 million. The Washington Post reported in 1993 that the Central African Republic had recognised it, and no other recognition is known.

Governments responded as they would to any fraud. In April 1998 the Marshall Islands condemned the claims as fraudulent, saying that those making them were not citizens and had no right to speak for Marshallese landowners. Pedley pleaded guilty to share manipulation in 2010, and his wife Pearlasia Gamboa, Melchizedek's president, lost a $1.8 million civil judgment that year.

Calling oneself a country gave none of these people any protection. Fraud law applies to the person selling the paper, wherever they say their nation is. It is not known to have been formally dissolved.

elgaland-vargaland.story:
The Kingdoms of Elgaland-Vargaland is an art project in the form of a country. The Swedish artists Carl Michael von Hausswolff and Leif Elggren made its name from their own and announced it in an advertisement in the newspaper Dagens Nyheter on 27 May 1992. They named themselves kings, in reaction to the fact that Sweden still has a monarchy.

Its constitution claims what other countries leave out, which is the border zones between all countries on Earth, plus sea strips up to 10 nautical miles wide outside every country's territorial waters. It also claims states of mind and unreal places, including the Hypnagogic State, the moment between waking and sleep, and a digital Virtual Room. All dead people count as citizens, and it reported 980 living citizens in 2014.

In practice it runs as an art project does. The founders issue a flag, anthem, stamps and passports on request. They hold exhibitions called embassies, including in Reykjavik in 1994, Berlin in 2006 and Morocco in 2014. They applied for United Nations membership in 1994, and no result is known.

In 2002 a group travelling on its passports was detained in Estonia and sent back to Sweden the next day, which is the one moment the project met a real border. No activity after 2014 is reported.

Since a border in law is a line with no width, there is no strip of land to claim, and no state has to respond. The project shows how far a declaration can go when nobody has to answer it, and the Estonian episode shows where it stops.

afropolitan.story:
Afropolitan is a company in the San Francisco Bay Area that has marketed itself as a digital nation for the African diaspora, people of African descent living outside the continent. It began in 2016 as a networking and events business for wealthy members of the diaspora. Eche Emole, one of its founders, was born in Lagos, Nigeria, and moved to the United States at 15. His co-founder is Chika Uwazie.

The nation idea came from the network state, a theory set out by the venture capitalist Balaji Srinivasan in a 2022 book. It holds that a community can form online around shared values and later grow into something like a country. In May 2022 the founders announced a four-part plan for what the tech news site Built In reported as the world's first digital nation, aimed at fostering the Black community. They compared it to Facebook as a country, with its own laws, currency and culture. The company raised $2.1 million in seed funding, the first money from early investors, and on 13 September 2022 Uwazie rang the closing bell at the New York Stock Exchange.

The plan belonged to Web3, a vision of an internet in which online communities use blockchain technology to take control from big tech companies. A critical 2025 article on the website Africa Is a Country looked at what had come of it after three years. It found that the founders ran a podcast and three services launched in late 2024, a dating service, paid mentoring and an event-booking app. The writer described it as a networking club for elites and said that the digital nation idea served as a hook for investors. The founders have described it differently, as the first stage of a long plan.

Afropolitan is not known to have any territory, passport or legal status. It is a company under the law of the place where it is registered, and its members remain citizens of their own countries. Calling a business a nation changes neither fact. The case shows how the language of founding a nation can serve as a marketing idea, and it gives no sign of any state treating the idea as more than that.

barbados-metaverse-embassy.story:
Barbados is a small Caribbean island country. In November 2021 it announced that it would open an embassy in the metaverse, meaning online 3D worlds where people move around as animated figures. An embassy is normally a building in a foreign capital, staffed by diplomats and protected by treaty, where a country deals with its host and helps its own citizens. Barbados wanted to see whether the same thing could exist in software.

On 14 November 2021 its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade signed an agreement with Decentraland, a virtual world with over 90,000 plots of land bought with cryptocurrency. Talks with two other platforms, Somnium Space and SuperWorld, were being finalised. Gabriel Abed, a crypto entrepreneur and Barbados's ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, brokered the deal. The embassy would offer services such as electronic visas, and the country planned to declare its virtual land sovereign, meaning under its own authority. Avinash Persaud, special envoy to Prime Minister Mia Mottley, called it the first official embassy or lookout post in the metaverse and promised a report in twelve months. A government statement said that it would support stronger relations with other governments.

Others were doubtful. A CoinDesk opinion piece called it a gimmick and asked why a website would not do. Timing slipped too. An opening was first expected around January 2022, in February a newsletter still described it as coming soon, and an article from June 2022 said it was tentatively scheduled for later that month. It has not been confirmed that the embassy opened or that the report appeared.

The legal point is about who has to agree. Embassies get their protections under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations because a host state agrees to receive them. In Decentraland no state is host, and the platform's rules are private. So Barbados could call its plot sovereign, but its declaration binds no one else, and no other country is reported to have accepted it. Barbados can offer any online service it wants, such as a visa application, because it is a recognised state acting on its own authority. The virtual building adds no legal power to that.

barlow-declaration.story:
In February 1996 the internet was new to most people, and governments had just begun passing laws about it. John Perry Barlow was a founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a group that campaigns for rights online. He published A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace on the web on 8 February 1996, from the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, for a project called 24 Hours in Cyberspace.

It is a short manifesto of sixteen brief paragraphs. It opens by addressing the "Governments of the Industrial World, you weary giants of flesh and steel" and tells them that they have no sovereignty, meaning legal authority, in the place where its authors meet. Barlow stated that the online world had no elected government and did not want one, that the United States lacked the consent of the governed to apply its laws there, and that the internet lay outside every country's borders.

It is the best-known claim of a place outside every country that has no land at all. It created no members, courts or money, and nobody could join or leave it. Its power was in the argument, namely that authority should rest on the consent of users and not on where they stand.

Governments have since acted against that claim, for a practical reason. The internet has physical parts, such as servers, satellites and ground stations, and these and the people who run them are located where a government can reach them. A court can order a company, seize a machine or arrest an operator. A person sitting at a keyboard is in a country, and that country's law applies to them whatever they feel about the screen. No government has accepted the declaration. Its text is still online at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and later projects, including Bitnation and the network state, make similar arguments.

estonia-data-embassy.story:
Estonia is a small Baltic country bordering Russia. It runs much of its government online, and that creates a specific risk. If its records live only on servers inside the country, an attack or occupation could destroy the land registry, the business registry and the other lists that let a state function. The Estonian government wanted those records to survive even if its own territory did not.

Work began in 2015. In 2017 Estonia and Luxembourg signed an agreement. Luxembourg was a natural choice, with 23 high-tech data centres and a record of storing data for NATO and the European Union. Estonia's servers sit in a high-security data centre there, whose exact location has not been disclosed, and they stay under Estonian control. Luxembourg's IT director Patrick Houtsch told NBC News that his government provided the data centre services along with immunity, and called that the innovative part. Immunity here means protection from local law, so Luxembourg's police or courts cannot simply seize the machines.

In June 2019 Estonia moved four core databases there, including land and business registries, with six more due by that September. The system can provide more than backups and is able to run the most critical services. The Estonian government calls it an extension of the state in the cloud and something new under international law. It draws on the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, the treaty that protects embassies, though it is not an embassy in the traditional sense, and the two countries' agreement is what gives it force.

This is the best working example of a state's functions existing outside its land. But look at how it was made. It begins with a recognised state, which obtains immunity by agreement with another recognised state, and depends on the host's continued consent. A private group could rent the same servers and would not get the immunity, because that comes only from a government's promise to another government. Estonia's government still describes the arrangement as running.

estonia-e-residency.mechanism: An existing country can offer legal identity and company law to people living elsewhere, online. This gives them much of what online nations promise, backed by a recognised state, and leaves them subject to the law of wherever they live.
estonia-e-residency.story:
Estonia is a small Baltic country that launched e-Residency at the end of 2014. The programme gives foreigners a secure digital identity, so that they can set up and run Estonian companies online without ever visiting. It is often mentioned alongside online nations, but it runs the other way around. A self-declared online nation has a community and no government. Here a real state hands out a digital status.

An e-resident gets a way to prove identity online and sign documents, and through that can register a company, deal with the tax office and run the business from anywhere. An e-resident does not become a citizen and does not get the right to live in Estonia, and the status is not a passport. Companies founded this way are ordinary Estonian companies under Estonian company and tax law.

The numbers are large for a country of its size. The official dashboard says over 144,000 people from 187 countries have become e-residents and have founded or co-founded more than 44,000 Estonian companies. In 2025 they set up a record 5,556 companies, up 15 percent from 2024. The state received nearly €125 million in direct revenue that year, made up of €54.5 million in labour taxes, €66 million in income tax mainly on dividends and €4.3 million in fees. The economy minister said every euro invested brought more than 12 back. Figures reported in September 2026 show over 4,200 new companies and about 9,000 new e-residents so far that year. Nearly half of the country's newly founded startups have an e-resident among their founders or board members.

Estonia does this because it brings in revenue and talent at little cost. The system works without land of its own because it relies on the territory, law, courts and banks Estonia already has. It gives people much of what online nations promise, a legal identity and a place to run a business, and it does so with a state's authority behind it. What it does not give is any freedom from the tax and legal duties of the country where the person actually lives. The programme continues to take new applicants.

liberland-metaverse.story:
Liberland is a self-declared country on Gornja Siga, an uninhabited stretch of floodplain on the Danube between Serbia and Croatia. The Czech activist Vít Jedlička declared it in 2015, arguing that the Croatia-Serbia border dispute left this patch unclaimed by either side. He describes a system of minimal government and an economy based on cryptocurrency. No state recognises it. Serbia's foreign ministry has called it a frivolous act needing no further comment. Croatia controls access, so supporters have had trouble even setting foot there.

A group that cannot reach its land can build somewhere else, and that was the point of the Liberland Metaverse. In early 2022 the architecture firm Zaha Hadid Architects, under its principal Patrik Schumacher, released designs for an online 3D city with curving buildings, a City Hall, a plaza and an exhibition centre, hosted on a platform called Mytaverse.

Buyers could purchase virtual land and set up businesses there, and they would also get a stake in the physical Liberland. Schumacher said the aim was to support Liberland's development as a libertarian micronation and to make a meeting place for cryptocurrency and online developers. He also argued that open virtual worlds run by their communities will beat those run by corporations. In November 2022 press reports still described Liberland as about to become a country in the metaverse. How many plots were sold, and whether the city is in use, is not known.

A virtual city gives people somewhere to gather and a project to invest in. It does nothing for the legal claim, which depends on whether real states accept Liberland and whether anyone can live on the floodplain.

nansen-passport.story:
A passport is a document issued by a government to its own citizens. Other countries honour it because they know which state stands behind the holder and will take them back. After the First World War, millions of people fell out of that system. Governments had fallen, borders had moved, and people were left without passports or a nation to issue them, which trapped them wherever they happened to be.

The sharpest case came in 1921, when the new Soviet government revoked the citizenship of Russians living abroad, including some 800,000 refugees from the Russian Civil War. These people could not cross a border legally, because no state would give them papers. The League of Nations, the international body before the United Nations, appointed the Norwegian explorer and statesman Fridtjof Nansen as its High Commissioner for Refugees. In July 1922 he called a conference in Geneva, and governments agreed on a travel document for stateless people. Officially a stateless persons passport, it quickly took his name.

It was extended to Armenian refugees in 1924 and to Assyrian, Bulgarian and Turkish ones in 1928. About 450,000 were issued. After Nansen died in 1930, the Nansen International Office for Refugees ran the system, and it won the 1938 Nobel Peace Prize, the year it closed. Later documents for refugees and stateless people now come from national and international authorities.

The document gave limited things. It let a person show who they were and cross a border, if the receiving state agreed. It did not give citizenship or the right to stay, and holders lived under the law of whichever state they had reached.

The Nansen passport shows that a travel document can work with no territory behind it. Compare it with Garry Davis's later World Passport, which also came from outside any state, and which governments had made no promise to accept. The Nansen passport's authority came from the governments that agreed in advance to honour it. Anyone hoping to issue passports for a new community needs that same agreement, and printing the booklet is the small part of the task.

network-state-school.story:
The Network State is an idea for starting new countries online, and the Network School is its test site. Balaji Srinivasan, former chief technology officer of the cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase, set out the idea in a 2022 book. An online community forms first around shared values, it pools money to buy land in scattered places, and it eventually seeks diplomatic recognition from real governments. This reverses the usual order, in which land comes first.

In August 2024 he announced the Network School in a hotel at Forest City, a half-empty development in Johor, Malaysia. It became permanent in May 2025. It was a private community where startup founders, engineers and other tech workers lived and worked together, paying about $1,500 to $3,000 a month. It was not a government-recognised university and gave no degrees. Srinivasan said over $100 million was committed to it. In law it was an ordinary business with a council licence, run in Malaysia under Malaysian licensing and immigration rules.

Then came trouble. Social media claims spread that Israelis had entered on second passports, a charged issue in Malaysia.
