Malaysian officers inspected the site on 14 July 2026, checked 266 foreigners from 40 countries and found all documents valid. Commentators also objected to its stated aims on sovereignty and asked how it came to operate there at all. Srinivasan suspended a planned $500 million investment. On 21 July the Iskandar Puteri City Council revoked the school's business licence, citing breaches of licence conditions and of how the premises could be used, and ordered it to stop the next day.

Within hours Kazakhstan's digital ministry signed a memorandum, a non-binding statement of intent, to host a campus. Network School Kazakhstan launched at a centre in Astana on 2 September 2026, with Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev taking part.

The episode gave the idea a real test. A community can begin online, but once it has rooms and residents it needs a host country, and a city council's ordinary licensing power was enough to close it in one day. Having money and members did not change that. The move shows the other side of the same position. A mobile community can leave for a government that wants it, and it will then live under that government's rules.

order-of-malta.story:
The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is the oldest and best-known answer to a question that runs through this whole subject, which is whether something can be sovereign without land. Sovereign means treated as an independent authority in international law, able to deal with states as an equal. The Order is a Catholic religious order with 39 vowed members and no territory of its own, and many countries treat it that way.

It began in the 11th century as a hospital community in Jerusalem, founded by a man known as Blessed Gerard, and Pope Paschal II approved it in 1113. As the Crusades went on it became a military order as well. It later ruled the island of Rhodes and then Malta, which it defended for more than three months against the Ottoman Empire in the Great Siege of 1565. For those centuries it was an ordinary territorial state.

In June 1798 Napoleon's forces took Malta and the Order lost its last territory. Then something unusual happened. Other countries went on treating it as a sovereign body, and it kept conducting diplomacy from its new base. It holds two headquarters buildings in Rome with extraterritorial status, meaning that Italian law treats them as outside normal Italian control, though they are not a territory the Order rules as a country.

Day to day it does what a state's foreign ministry does. It issues its own passports, coins and stamps, and it signs treaties. Its website reports diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the European Union, while Wikipedia gives 115 states. The United Nations General Assembly made it a permanent observer in 1994, citing its humanitarian work. Only three of its senior officers count as its citizens, so no population depends on it. The rest of its members are citizens of ordinary countries. It says its diplomatic network exists to give its medical programmes protected access in crisis regions, and its hospitals and aid work supply the reason for states to keep the relationship going.

People who want a state without land often point to the Order. Its case is hard to copy. Its status rests on some nine centuries of history, on having once really ruled territory, on the Catholic Church's support and on a stream of aid work that governments value. Its recognition was inherited from a time when it held land, and no group has been shown to gain the same treatment from scratch. It shows that diplomatic recognition can outlast territory, as long as enough states choose to continue it.

pirate-party-hosting.story:
The Pirate Bay was a Swedish website for finding shared files, many of them copyrighted films and music. Sites in legal trouble have sometimes looked for a far-off country or an offshore platform to keep their servers on. In 2010 the Swedish Pirate Party, a small political party that campaigns against strict copyright law, tried something else. It looked for protection inside Sweden's own legal system.

The party became The Pirate Bay's internet provider that year, the company whose network carries a site to the public. Its founder, Rick Falkvinge, later described the step as politically provocative and as a legal shield for the site, because anyone trying to cut it off would now be dealing with a political party.

In July 2010 the party went further. It proposed that if it won seats in the Swedish parliament on 19 September, it would host The Pirate Bay from inside the building. Its argument rested on a rule protecting members of parliament from prosecution for political acts in their work. Falkvinge wrote that because the party had made hosting an election promise, it would count as political activity and so be constitutionally protected. Whether a court would have accepted this was never tested, because the plan needed seats. The party won 0.65 percent and no seats.

The party also offered hosting and bandwidth to WikiLeaks, through its vice chairman Anna Troberg, and launched an anonymous internet provider. In 2013 Falkvinge wrote that The Pirate Bay's address still ended at the party's network. The site later moved to many places, including encrypted cloud services.

This entry stands in contrast to the Sealand kind of story. It used no ocean and no unclaimed land. The idea was that the strongest shelter might be a state's own rules about its own lawmakers. That kind of shelter depends on an election and on how judges read the rule, so its limit was reached on election night.

praxis.why: Wikipedia also names David Weinreb as a co-founder.
praxis.story:
Praxis is a New York company that has spent years looking for a place to build a new city on its own terms. Dryden Brown and Charlie Callinan founded it in 2019, and Wikipedia also names David Weinreb as a founder. Brown had been homeschooled for competitive surfing, read Ayn Rand and Austrian economists, left New York University, and worked at a hedge fund, where he met Callinan, a former college football player. He was fired from the fund. The company plans a city of 10,000 people, and the story of Praxis is largely the story of where that city might go.

The first trip came in 2019, when Brown and Callinan went to Nigeria and Ghana, paid for with money Callinan had won in a golf tournament, and proposed a financial centre to Ghana's vice-president, Mahamudu Bawumia. The firm then described plans in the Mediterranean, followed by Greenland. In 2024 Gizmodo, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported $525 million in new funding. Of this, $500 million was a drawdown facility from the crypto firm GEM Digital, meaning money that is released only once conditions are met, here the listing of Praxis tokens on a public exchange. So most of the headline figure depended on a future event.

Also in 2024 Brown wrote that he had flown to Nuuk to try to buy Greenland. He told TechCrunch he hoped to work with the government on a new city on uninhabitable land. Danish MP Rasmus Jarlov replied that Greenlandic independence needs the Danish parliament's approval and a change to the constitution, so it was not something a visiting company could arrange.

In June 2025 Vanity Fair reported that Brown had chosen a site at Vandenberg, a US Space Force base in California, for a city called Atlas. On 22 September 2026 Praxis announced a deal to build inside +Colonia, a 515-hectare development near Colonia del Sacramento in Uruguay. The New York Times described the agreement as largely non-binding. Praxis plans to start buying land by the end of 2027.

No Praxis city has been built. Each site has required a host government's agreement, and each time the plan has changed. The case shows the order of problems a land-less venture faces. Raising money and members is possible, and it still leaves the venture needing a state to let it build under that state's law.

second-life-embassies.story:
Second Life is an online 3D world, launched in the 2000s, where people move around as animated figures and build things. In 2007 a few real countries opened embassies there. An ordinary embassy has legal protections and handles diplomacy, and these did neither.

Sweden announced its plan in January 2007. It was to open on 30 May with a copy of the House of Sweden, its real embassy building in Washington, built through the Swedish Institute, a government body that promotes the country abroad, for 400,000 kronor, about $57,000. The announcement drew international attention. The Maldives, an island country in the Indian Ocean, got there a few days earlier and put its own embassy on Diplomacy Island, a virtual diplomatic quarter. Foreign Minister Carl Bildt then opened Sweden's in a ceremony held both online and in person. Estonia joined later that year, with Foreign Minister Urmas Paet citing the importance of the internet for communication and planning lectures and art shows.

These countries used the embassies for publicity and cultural outreach, much as they would use a website or a stand at a trade fair. They added nothing to anyone's legal status and created no territory. An embassy's protections in law come from an agreement between the two countries involved, and here no host state existed. Whether any still operates is not known. These cases came well before Barbados announced its metaverse embassy in 2021, and they show that the idea had been tried and what it amounted to.

tuvalu-digital-nation.story:
Tuvalu is a recognised Pacific country of about 12,000 people, spread over low-lying islands that the United Nations Development Programme classes as extremely vulnerable to climate change. The Rising Nations Initiative says that small island nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands are likely to become uninhabitable within a few decades. That raises a question international law has never had to answer, which is what happens to a country when its land goes under water.

The usual test for a state, set out in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the ability to deal with other states. Territory is on that list. So on one reading Tuvalu could lose its legal existence along with its homes.

At the COP27 climate conference in November 2022 its Foreign Minister, Simon Kofe, appeared in a video standing knee deep in the ocean. He said the country would move its land, ocean and culture to the cloud, as what it called the first digital nation. The plan, part of the Future Now Project, is to map all 124 islands and islets and to record cultural objects, language, elders' stories and dances, so that people abroad and future generations can keep them.

The legal step is the more important one. Tuvalu has asked other countries to agree in advance that it stays a state whatever happens to its land. Australia's Law Society Journal reported that 26 countries, including New Zealand and Australia, had legally recognised its digital statehood by December 2023, with a goal of 50. Australia also offered residency to 280 Tuvaluans a year. In its climate advisory opinion of July 2025 the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court, said that the disappearance of one of a state's parts "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". An advisory opinion does not bind states, though it carries weight.

The land is still there and the question has not been tested. The case differs from every self-declared internet nation in one way. Tuvalu starts as a full state with UN membership and is seeking to keep that status, so the digital record is a supplement to recognition it already has. Its strategy shows where the law's flexibility lies. States may be able to preserve a state by agreement, and this does not open the door for a new one to be created online.

wirtland.story:
Wirtland was a self-declared country that existed only on the internet, founded on 14 August 2008. It called itself the first internet-based sovereign state and an experiment on whether a country can be legitimate without land. Its own announcement in 2009 claimed about 700 citizens from all five continents. Who ran it is not clear beyond a description of it as a public initiative.

To give itself a physical presence it sold real objects. These included silver coins struck with its web address, including a 2009 piece showing a crane, stamps, and a national identity card open to anyone over 18. These items worked as collectibles and proved nothing legally, because a government's papers matter only when other governments accept them.

In January 2010 Wirtland issued a press release saying it had approached Nauru, a small Pacific island country, with a proposal to transfer a piece of its territory. Susan Simpson, writing on the international law blog The View From LL2, noted that Nauru had recently recognised the breakaway region of Abkhazia, and that its recognition had gone to the highest bidder before. She still said the scheme could never work. Wirtland, she wrote, was no sovereign, with few citizens and no power to tax.

No land is known to have changed hands, and no activity is known in 2026. The request says the most. A project built on the idea that a state needs no territory ended up asking for some, which concedes the point it set out to disprove.

world-service-authority.story:
The World Service Authority is an organisation in Washington, DC, that issues a World Passport and other papers to people who call themselves citizens of the world. Its founder, Garry Davis, was a former Broadway performer and American bomber pilot in the Second World War. 

On 25 May 1948 he walked into the American embassy in Paris and gave up his US citizenship, saying that he was a citizen of the world. That left him stateless, with no country obliged to admit him. That November he stormed a session of the United Nations General Assembly in Paris. In 1949 he founded the International Registry of World Citizens, and on 4 September 1953 he declared the World Government of World Citizens, with the Authority as its administrative arm.

The Authority issued passports, identity cards and birth and marriage certificates, for fees, and occasionally currency and stamps. The New York Times wrote in his 2013 obituary that over 2.5 million documents had been issued and 950,000 people registered. It has no territory and does not claim to rule anyone's land.

Whether it helps depends on who is asked. Supporters said the papers helped refugees and stateless people, who have no other document to show. Critics said Davis charged poor people for papers legally recognised almost nowhere, and others list it as a fantasy document. Foreign Policy reported that a small handful of countries accepted the passport, while the Authority claims 189 countries have at some time stamped one. A stamp may mean only that one officer on one day accepted it, so the two figures measure different things.

Davis travelled on it for 65 years and was regularly arrested and expelled. He died in Vermont in July 2013, aged 91, shortly after sending passports to Julian Assange and Edward Snowden.

His life is the long test of this idea. A passport is a request from one authority to another, so it works only where a border officer chooses to honour it. The League of Nations' Nansen passport worked because governments had agreed in advance to accept it. Davis had no such agreement, so he depended on each officer's discretion, and that is also what his customers got.

freedomland-kalayaan.story:
The Spratly Islands are hundreds of small islands, reefs and shoals in the South China Sea, west of the Philippines, claimed in whole or part by several countries. Before the Second World War Japan held them. In the 1951 San Francisco peace treaty Japan gave up the islands, and the treaty did not say who got them. That gap was what Tomás Cloma saw.

Cloma was a Filipino businessman who owned a fishing fleet and a maritime school. His brother Filemon reportedly found the area when a typhoon pushed his boats west of Palawan in 1947. On 11 May 1956 Filemon led 40 men in taking formal possession of 53 islands and islets some 380 miles west of Palawan, and they posted a Notice to the Whole World. Tomás argued that the area had no owner because Japan had given it up. He declared the Free Territory of Freedomland on 21 May, naming a government, with a capital on Flat Island from July.

Other governments were not willing to leave it empty. In October 1956 Taiwanese naval ships met Filemon's boat at North Danger Reef, and Taiwan later burned buildings and took property. A private group had no way to stand up to a navy. So the brothers asked the Philippine government for support.

The government took its time, and then turned on him. In 1972 President Ferdinand Marcos jailed Tomás for four months for impersonating an officer by using the title admiral. In August 1974 the group adopted a new constitution and renamed the territory Colonia. That December Tomás was arrested again and made to sign over his rights to the Philippines for one peso. A 1978 decree made the area the Municipality of Kalayaan, which the Philippines still counts as its own.

Here the private claim did not fail outright. It was taken over. Cloma's act of occupation and his notice to the world, worthless to him against a navy, had value to a state, and the Philippines cites the 1974 transfer as one basis for its own title. Other claimants do not accept it. The case shows one way a private occupation of unowned land can end, with a nearby government using the claim for itself and paying the claimant one peso.

kingdom-of-enenkio.story:
Wake Island is a remote Pacific atoll, a ring of coral, with no native population. The United States has controlled it since 1899. The Marshall Islands, a Pacific nation to the south, also claims it, calling it Ānen Kio. In 1973 Marshallese lawmakers declared that it had always belonged to their people, a claim resting on oral legends and songs.

The Kingdom of EnenKio grew out of that dispute without being part of it. In 1994 Robert F. Moore, a Honolulu resident who said he acted for a Marshallese chief, Murjel Hermios, announced that an independent kingdom existed on Wake and four other atolls, which he said the United States had seized from their rightful native owners. He called himself Minister Plenipotentiary, a title for a senior envoy, and the kingdom issued passports. In 1997 the Marshall Islands Journal reported that it had declared war on the United States and was asking for Marshallese support.

The people it claimed to speak for rejected it. On 23 April 1998 the Marshall Islands government issued a formal note condemning its claims, saying that its representatives were not citizens and had no right to speak for Marshallese landowners.

Moore then turned to investors. He marketed $1 billion in Enenkio Gold War Bonds online, saying they were backed by gold and promising 10 percent compound interest after five years. This brought him under US investment law, which requires bonds offered to the public to be registered and forbids false statements about them. The Securities and Exchange Commission, the American regulator of investments, said no gold or other backing existed and that the bonds had not been registered. In October 2000 it won a court order from Judge Susan Mollway in Honolulu that froze his assets and required him to account for the money. How the case ended is not known.

No state recognises the kingdom. It shows that a seller's claim to be a foreign government does not protect him from the regulator of the place where he actually sits.

mcclean-rockall.story:
Rockall is a bare granite rock about 17 metres high in the North Atlantic, 301 kilometres west of the Scottish island of Soay, and it is uninhabitable. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972. Ireland has never claimed the rock itself but disputes Britain's position.

Why anyone would care comes down to what a rock can generate at sea. Under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the main treaty on ocean rights, a country's land gives it an exclusive economic zone, a belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles wide where it controls fish and minerals, and rights over the nearby seabed, called the continental shelf. But a rock that cannot support human life or economic activity of its own gets neither. So whether people can live on Rockall may affect who controls a large area of sea.

Tom McClean set out to help Britain's side of that question. Abandoned as a baby in Dublin and raised at first in an orphanage, he served in Britain's Parachute Regiment and Special Air Service and became a survival expert. He is the opposite of a breakaway founder, because he went to reinforce an existing state's claim. He lived on the rock from 26 May to 4 July 1985, in what one account calls a wooden box, a record 40 days alone.

The claim that his stay reaffirmed Britain's title has been questioned, and a single person with supplies brought in does not show that a place can support human life. The record did not stand. Greenpeace activists passed it in 1997 with 42 days, and Nick Hancock reached 45 days alone in 2014. Britain still claims the rock and 12 nautical miles of sea around it, and Ireland still disputes this. McClean's stay shows how far people will go to give a rock legal weight, and it did not settle the question.

morac-songhrati-meads.story:
The Spratly Islands are a group of reefs and islets in the South China Sea that several countries dispute. The Republic of Morac-Songhrati-Meads was a claim to them that existed only on paper. Its supporters said that a British sea captain, James George Meads, had claimed the islands in 1877 and called himself King James I, and that a rival branch of the family formed a Kingdom of Humanity in 1914.

None of this has been shown to be true. The first evidence that can be checked comes from 1946, when Morton F. Meads, the captain's supposed descendant and an American soldier, was discharged in Manila over illegal private business, mainly reselling army surplus. Philippine newspapers printed his stories about a family birthright.

Those stories had an unexpected effect. They drew the attention of Filipino businessmen such as Tomás Cloma, who then raced to claim the islands for the Philippines. Cloma's claim later fed into the Philippine government's own argument for ruling part of the Spratlys.

The Meads group itself never set up a settlement, and its activity was limited to items such as postage stamps. Meads asked the United Nations, the Republic of China and the Philippines for recognition in 1972 and got nowhere. By one account, the rest of its governing body drowned that year when Typhoon Ora sank their ship. In 1985 he sued the United States and others for $25 billion, and the case was never heard. His descendants were still making the claim in the 1990s.

A family story with no documents and no one living on the land carries no legal weight, since a claim to territory needs actual possession and a state's authority. The case matters mainly for the rival claim it reportedly prompted.

principality-of-trinidad.story:
Trindade is a small uninhabited island in the South Atlantic, off the coast of Brazil. James Harden-Hickey was born in San Francisco in 1854, raised in France, and became a writer, newspaper editor and duellist. He saw the island on a voyage and treated it as terra nullius, a legal term for land that belongs to no one. Under old rules, such land could be claimed by whoever occupied it first.

In 1893 he proclaimed himself James I, Prince of Trinidad, and planned a military dictatorship under his own rule. He designed stamps, a flag and a coat of arms, founded a knightly order, bought a schooner to carry colonists and opened a consular office in New York. He sold government bonds to pay for building on the island, in an amount that is unknown. No settlers are confirmed to have lived there.

The plan ended because the island turned out to matter to someone else. In 1895 The New York Times reported that the British warship Barracouta had taken possession while he was in California. Britain wanted it as a station for a telegraph cable and based its claim on a visit by the astronomer Edmund Halley in 1700. Harden-Hickey appealed to the United States government without result.

Brazil then pressed its own claim, based on Portuguese discovery in 1502, and won the dispute with Britain through diplomacy. The Brazilian state of Espírito Santo put up a marker in January 1897, and Harden-Hickey died in El Paso, Texas, in February 1898. Trindade remains Brazilian, and the Brazilian navy keeps a post there.

Harden-Hickey never lost in any court. He was simply left out of the argument once two governments became interested. The term terra nullius assumes that nobody holds a claim, and old claims of discovery could outweigh a later proclamation.

waveland-rockall.story:
Rockall is a small granite rock in the North Atlantic, about 301 kilometres from the nearest Scottish island of Soay. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972. Ireland, Iceland and Denmark have contested the rights around it, because whoever holds it might claim the surrounding seabed, where there may be oil.

The environmental group Greenpeace chose it for that reason. In the mid-1990s it was campaigning against oil exploration in the Atlantic, including a £1 billion field run by the oil company BP, and BP was at the same time seeking to sue four of its members for £1.4 million over an earlier protest. On 11 June 1997 activists landed on the rock. Three or four at a time stayed for 42 days, a record then.

They declared Rockall the capital of the Global State of Waveland and offered citizenship to anyone who would take a pledge of allegiance. It was a protest in the form of a country. John Vidal, one of those who landed, said the team unscrewed the 1955 British plaque and refixed it back to front. The Flags of the World website says that Prime Minister Tony Blair refused their petition for recognition.

The British government's reply was the most instructive part. It said that Rockall was British territory and that anyone was free to go there and stay as long as they pleased. By treating the occupiers as ordinary visitors on British soil, it never had to act against them or take the claim seriously. No force was used. Greenpeace used the occupation as a base for actions against rigs and ships surveying for oil, and landed again in 1998.

Waveland has no standing in any country's law, and Britain still holds Rockall. The episode shows that declaring a state can succeed as publicity, and that a government can defeat the legal claim simply by ignoring it.

kiribati-floating-islands.story:
Kiribati is a nation of low-lying islands in the central Pacific Ocean, threatened by rising seas. Its government has had to ask what it would do if its land became unlivable, and this entry records one answer from 2011.

In September that year, at the Pacific Islands Forum in New Zealand, President Anote Tong told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that his government was considering everything, including floating islands, because it was running out of options. He compared the idea to oil drilling rigs and asked what any person would do if the choice was to be submerged with their family or to climb onto a rig. He put the cost at about $2 billion, which would have to come from other countries. He named no site and showed no design.

Three years later his government took a different path and bought land in Fiji, another Pacific country, a parcel of about 22 square kilometres. That gave ownership of land under Fiji's law. Later president Taneti Maamau announced that China would help farm it. No platform was ever built.

The law adds another difficulty. Under Article 60(8) of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the main treaty on ocean rights, an artificial island is not an island. It has no territorial sea of its own, meaning the band of coastal water a country fully controls. So a platform would house people, but it would not by itself carry the sea rights that Kiribati's natural land now gives it. It would also have to float somewhere, and if in another country's waters that country would decide what happened.

The proposal shows the options open to a small state facing this. Each one, whether a rig or a farm abroad, depends on someone else's money or someone else's land.

xlii-seastead-phuket.story:
A seastead is a permanent home at sea, and its backers hope to live beyond any country's laws. XLII was a small one, a six-metre-wide cabin raised on a weighted column, paid for and built by a company called Ocean Builders. It was anchored in the Andaman Sea about 14 nautical miles off Phuket, Thailand. Chad Elwartowski, a 46-year-old American bitcoin trader, and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet moved in during early 2019.

The location was chosen with the law of the sea in mind. A country's full territorial sea ends 12 nautical miles from its coast. From 12 to 24 miles is the contiguous zone, where it has only limited powers such as customs enforcement. Out to 200 miles is the exclusive economic zone, where it controls fish and minerals. Ocean Builders and its supporters relied on the limits these rules place on a coastal state past 12 miles. Elwartowski said 20 more homes would be sold to form a community.

Thailand disagreed. The Thai navy said that the couple had announced autonomy beyond the reach of any court and invited others to join, and it treated this as an attack on the country's sovereignty, its right to rule its own territory. The couple left before the navy raided the cabin on 13 April 2019. Thailand revoked Elwartowski's visa and charged the two under a law carrying life in prison or death. On 22 April navy boats began towing the cabin to shore as evidence.

Ocean Builders said that the cabin sat in the contiguous zone and that no micronation was intended. Thailand pointed to its 200-mile economic zone. A senior official urged the couple to come back and fight the charge in court. In June 2019 officials said there had been no progress in arresting them, after tracing them to Tarutao island in April. In July prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged, among them seven Thais and a German. How the case ended is not known.

The treaty does limit what a state may do past 12 miles, but a state that sees a threat can act first and argue later, and those living on the platform carried the risk. Their case also shows the problem of ties to land, since Thepdet was a Thai citizen and Elwartowski held a Thai visa, and that gave Thailand direct power over them whatever the status of the water.

central-tibetan-administration.story:
Tibet is a high plateau region in Asia, under Chinese control. In 1951 Tibet's leaders and China signed the Seventeen Point Agreement, which placed Tibet under China. In March 1959 the 14th Dalai Lama, Tibet's religious leader and then its head of government, fled to India and rejected that agreement. That April he re-established his cabinet, the Kashag, in exile. The Central Tibetan Administration is what grew from it, and it is based in Dharamshala in northern India.

A government in exile is a body that claims to speak for a people or country while unable to govern that land. This one has built most of the machinery of a state. It has courts, a parliament and an executive, under a charter adopted in 1991. In 2011 the Dalai Lama gave up his political duties, and executive power passed to an elected leader called the Sikyong. Penpa Tsering was sworn in for a second five-year term in May 2026.

It has no land, so it reaches people another way. Tibetans abroad vote for the parliament and the Sikyong and make yearly contributions recorded in the Green Book, a document sometimes called a passport, though it does not let anyone cross a border. Money comes mainly from private donations, these contributions and aid from governments such as India and the United States.

What it lacks is legal standing as a state. No country recognises the administration as a sovereign government, meaning one with the legal right to rule Tibet, although it receives aid for welfare work. It exists on Indian soil by India's permission, and its members live under Indian law or that of the country they have moved to. It continues to hold elections.

The case shows how much of a government can be carried without territory. Elections, taxes in the form of voluntary contributions and a court system can all exist if people want them. What cannot be built this way is the power to rule the land, or the recognition of other states.

rada-of-belarusian-republic.story:
Belarus is a country in eastern Europe, between Poland and Russia. The Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic, also known as the Belarusian People's Republic, is a council that has claimed to represent it from exile for more than a century. A rada is a council. It calls itself the oldest existing government in exile.

It began in Minsk in 1918, during the First World War, when German forces occupied the area. The Rada of the All-Belarusian Congress expanded into a temporary parliament, and on 25 March 1918 it adopted a charter proclaiming independence and appealed for international recognition. Germany did not officially recognise it, although the Rada had diplomatic contacts with neighbours such as Finland, the Ukrainian People's Republic and the Baltic states. It had a brief window while empires were collapsing and new states were appearing.

When Bolshevik armies advanced at the end of 1918 it left Minsk, moving through Grodno and Vilnius to Kaunas, and it has been in exile since 1919. Belarus became a Soviet republic. A Red Army advance in 1945 forced the Rada to move again, to western Germany.

Today it works as an advocacy group among Belarusians in North America, Britain and elsewhere, meeting in diaspora facilities, and presses Western officials to support Belarusian independence and democracy. Ivonka Survilla has been its president since 1997. It says it holds a symbolic mandate that it wants to hand to a democratically elected Belarusian parliament. It supported the opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya during the 2020–2021 protests, and the Belarusian KGB declared it an extremist group in June 2023.

It holds no territory, issues nothing with legal force and governs no one. The case shows what a claim to represent a country can come down to after a very long time, which is a group of people abroad keeping a name, a flag and a cause alive. Being declared extremist at home shows that its old opponent still treats it as worth attention.

a23a-iceberg.story:
A23a was the largest iceberg in the world for much of its life, and it carried away part of a Soviet research base. It is included because people sometimes imagine ice as ground that could host a new settlement, and this iceberg's history shows how that goes.

An ice shelf is a floating sheet of ice attached to a continent, and pieces break off it, which is called calving. In 1986 A23a calved from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in Antarctica. The Soviet base Druzhnaya I stood on that part of the shelf, so the base went with it, and a rescue mission began in 1987 to move what could be saved. Rusted debris from the base could still be seen in the edge of the ice in January 2025.

The iceberg then sat stuck on the sea bed for many years and began moving in 2020. In January 2025 it measured about 3,500 square kilometres. It spun over an undersea mountain through much of 2024, then grounded 73 kilometres from the island of South Georgia in March 2025 and floated off again by July.

Once it left the cold Antarctic waters it went quickly. By September 2025 it was breaking up in warmer water, and in March 2026 its largest piece was down to 180 square kilometres. Formal monitoring then stopped, and by July 2026 it was thought to be gone or nearly so.

So the largest iceberg known lasted about 40 years, and most of those were spent aground. Anything built on it would have moved wherever the ocean sent it, with no way to steer it and no sign of when it would break apart. No one has claimed it as a country, and an iceberg of this type gives no one a lasting place to stand.

camp-barneo.story:
Camp Barneo was a private tourist camp built each spring on floating sea ice in the Arctic Ocean near the North Pole, in waters beyond any country's land. For a few weeks each April it was the northernmost inhabited place in the world.

The Russian Alexander Orlov founded it in 2002. His widow Irina Orlova ran it after him, then sold it to the Swedish pharmaceutical billionaire Frederik Paulsen. It ran under the patronage of the Russian Geographical Society. Because the ice keeps moving, the camp had to be rebuilt from nothing each April, and in 2007 winds pushed it southeast at 0.8 kilometres an hour. A visit cost about $20,000.

There is no land there, so at first glance no one governs the place. But from 2002 to 2017 every trip started and ended at Longyearbyen on Svalbard, a Norwegian archipelago, so the camp relied on Norway for its flights. This turned out to be its weak point. In 2016, after Chechen paratroopers held military exercises at Barneo, Norway imposed a flight ban, which it later lifted. A dispute between Russia and Ukraine stopped tourist flights in 2019. COVID-19 cancelled the 2020 and 2021 seasons, plans for 2022 ended with Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and a 2024 season meant to leave from Russia was also cancelled. The camp last operated in 2018.

The Arctic Council's senior officials once met there, which shows that it was treated as useful, and the camp never claimed independence. The case gives a plain lesson for anyone hoping to operate beyond every country. The ice may be outside national territory, while the airport, the fuel and the permits are all inside it, and whoever controls those can close the operation without touching the ice.

north-pole-drift-stations.story:
Sea ice in the Arctic Ocean is not fixed. It floats and drifts with wind and current, so a camp placed on it moves too. The North Pole stations are research camps the Soviet Union, and later Russia, has placed on this ice to study the ocean and weather. During the Cold War both the Soviet Union and the United States kept such stations, for research and also for espionage.

On 21 May 1937 the Soviet Union set up North Pole-1 on an ice floe about 20 kilometres from the Pole, in an expedition led by Otto Schmidt. Four men lived there for nine months while the floe drifted 2,850 kilometres, until icebreaker ships took them off in February 1938. They came home as Heroes of the Soviet Union.

From 1954, one to three stations ran each year. A typical camp began in April and lasted two or three years, until its floe reached the Greenland Sea, and North Pole-22 drifted for nine years. About 800 people have worked on the stations since 1937, replaced each year. The Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute, a single government body, has run them all.

The program stopped after the Soviet Union ended and resumed in 2003. From the mid-2000s it became hard to find a safe floe, and several stations were evacuated early because the ice melted too fast. Russia therefore ordered a self-propelled, ice-resistant platform called North Pole in 2017, to replace camps on bare ice. It was completed in August 2022, ran station NP-41 from 2022 to 2024 and started NP-42 in 2024.

These stations show that people can live on drifting ice for years. They also show the cost of doing so. They needed a government's budget and a chain of supply, and they stayed state property the whole time. No one on them claimed to be outside Russian authority. With the ice thinning, even that government has moved its station onto a ship.

project-habakkuk.story:
Project Habakkuk was a British plan during the Second World War to build a giant aircraft carrier out of ice. In the mid-Atlantic, German U-boats operated beyond the flight range of planes based on land, and Britain needed a way to bring planes there. Geoffrey Pyke, who worked at Britain's Combined Operations Headquarters under Lord Louis Mountbatten, proposed levelling an iceberg, natural or artificial, into an airbase.

The scientist Max Perutz warned in 1942 that real icebergs have too little surface above water and can roll over. The idea survived because of pykrete, named after Pyke, a frozen mix of water and wood pulp that was stronger than ice and slower to melt. The plan then became a ship 600 metres long, far larger than any vessel built.

The difficulties came with testing. Pykrete still sagged slowly unless kept at minus 16 degrees Celsius, so the vessel would have needed insulation and refrigeration, which meant it was no longer a simple block of ice. A prototype 18 metres by 9 metres, weighing 1,000 tons, was built on Patricia Lake in Jasper National Park, Alberta, Canada.

As the work went on, the estimated cost grew from £700,000 to £2.5 million, and Canada said it could not be done that season. Meanwhile, longer-range aircraft and escort carriers closed the gap in the Atlantic that had made the project necessary. The project's board last met in December 1943 and called the large ship impractical, so it was never built.

The project is included because it is the largest ice platform anyone has seriously planned. Even with a wartime government's science and money, it could not be done at a sensible cost. It also would have had no separate legal status, since a warship under Britain's flag is under British law wherever it floats.

uae-iceberg-project.story:
The United Arab Emirates is a desert country on the Persian Gulf that depends heavily on machinery to turn seawater into drinking water. Icebergs are nearly pure frozen fresh water, and the idea of towing one has been around for decades. In 1977 Saudi Arabia's Prince Mohammad al Faisal set up a company, Iceberg Transport International, for the same purpose, and that plan was never carried out.

Abdulla Alsheni, an Emirati businessman who owned National Adviser Bureau Limited, announced a new version in 2017. An iceberg would come from the area of Heard Island in the Southern Ocean to the coast of Fujairah and might yield 20 billion gallons of water. He presented it to two UAE ministries, with a trial planned for early 2022 and a final tow in late 2023, at a cost of $100 to 150 million.

The legal question is who owns an iceberg. The project's website claimed that under the freedom of the high seas, the rule that open ocean belongs to no country, anyone may take icebergs for private use. In a 2022 article in the journal Ius Novum, the legal writer Mateusz Osiecki tested that claim. He concluded that a free-floating iceberg is probably no state's property and noted that writers hold three different views. He also set out the duties under the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty, the rules protecting the Antarctic environment. He noted that the UAE belongs to neither the Antarctic Treaty system nor the Law of the Sea treaty, the main agreement on the oceans, which affects which of those duties apply to it.

No treaty names the owner of a floating iceberg, and no court has ruled on the point. No tow is known to have taken place, so the argument remains untested. It belongs here as a case where ice is treated as a resource to be taken, the reverse of treating it as a place to live.

bogota-declaration.story:
Geostationary orbit is a ring about 36,000 kilometres above the equator. A satellite placed there circles at the same speed the Earth turns, so it seems to stay fixed over one spot. That makes it very useful for communications and broadcasting, and only a limited number of satellites fit without interfering with each other.

By the 1970s the countries that had satellites were mostly rich ones. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty says that space cannot be claimed by any country. Eight equatorial countries thought that this arrangement favoured those already up there. Many of them were newly independent and resented a rule set by others. From 29 November to 3 December 1976 representatives of Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Congo, Zaire, Uganda, Kenya and Indonesia met in Bogotá, Colombia, and signed a declaration.

It called the orbit a scarce natural resource, and said that the part above each signer's territory fell under that country's sovereignty, meaning its full legal control. Parts over the open ocean were to be the common heritage of mankind, run by all nations together. To get around the treaty, the signers pointed out that it never defined where outer space begins. They argued that the orbit depends on Earth's gravity and so is not part of outer space, and that the treaty therefore did not cover the orbit above their land.

The claim won little support elsewhere. Other countries went on treating the orbit as space, and the International Telecommunication Union went on allotting positions in it by application. Two signers kept the claim in their law. Article 101 of Colombia's constitution lists its segment of the orbit as part of the country, and Colombia's Constitutional Court said in 2004 that the country had not given up sovereignty over it. Article 4 of Ecuador's 2008 constitution also asserts rights over the orbit.

It is one of the few direct challenges to the Outer Space Treaty, and the signers were recognised states making the argument in a formal way. They still could not change the rule alone. A state can write anything into its own constitution, but its claim over a satellite in orbit has force only if others accept it. No state operating a satellite there is known to have accepted it.

tongasat.story:
Geostationary orbit is the ring above the equator where a satellite stays over one spot. Space cannot be owned, but positions there must be shared out so that signals do not interfere. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a United Nations agency, keeps the register. Only countries can apply, and a position then belongs in practice to that country to use or license. Tonga is a small kingdom in the South Pacific, and Tongasat is the company that turned this rule into a business. It has been described as a flag of convenience for space, the way a ship might register in a small country.

In 1987 Matt Nilson, a businessman who had moved to Tonga from San Diego to retire, persuaded the king, through Princess Pilolevu, that even a tiny country could apply. The government authorised the venture in April 1988, and in March 1990 Nilson applied for 16 of the 180 slots then available. Intelsat, a satellite operator, and the United States objected. The ITU agreed in March 1991 after he cut the request to six, and Tonga eventually held nine, which made it the sixth-largest claimant of orbital slots. The plan was to rent each slot for $2 million a year, with half the profit going to the government.

A company called Rimsat rented slots in 1992, and Nilson was fired in February 1994 after an audit found that he owned Rimsat shares. In 2002 Tongasat launched the Esiafi 1 satellite. China later wanted the slot at 130 degrees East, and Tonga gave way in exchange for grant aid. Part of that money went to Tongasat rather than to the public, and it was challenged in court. On 17 August 2018 Lord Chief Justice Paulsen ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money.

In 2019 the court refused Tongasat's request to bring new evidence to its appeal and ordered it to pay about $15,000 as security for costs by 1 November, or the appeal would be put on hold. How the appeal finally ended is not known.

Tongasat shows the legal way a tiny place can earn from space. A rule that treats every recognised state alike gave Tonga standing that no private company could get. It also shows that the right still belongs to the state. A private group with no country behind it could file nothing, and the Tonga case shows the risks that arise when a state hands that right to a private agent, including conflicts of interest and fights over whose money it is.

oceania-atlantis-project.story:
The Atlantis Project was a plan to build a new country called Oceania on platforms in the Caribbean Sea off Panama. Eric Klien started it in February 1993, after he said election fraud had cost a Libertarian candidate, Tamara Clark, a Nevada state senate race. He wanted a place to start government over.

Oceania was to begin as about 80 hexagon-shaped units that fit together, holding 10,000 to 30,000 people. The project's own online guide priced the start at roughly one billion dollars and placed the site about fifty miles northeast of Panama, on water it described as 100 feet deep, near trade routes, in an area it said had no recorded hurricanes. It published a full constitution and legal code before anything was built, under the slogan "Break the Chains". Most of the activity was writing, and promotion ran largely through mailing lists and an online discussion group.

Klien later told VICE that the main reason it failed was too little interest, and that reaching people before the web was costly, through phones and newspaper advertisements. The project's guide says that it collapsed in April 1994. Klien went on to run the Lifeboat Foundation.

The site raises a legal point that would have come up if anything had floated. A country fully controls its coastal waters out to 12 nautical miles. A site 50 miles off Panama was outside that, but still inside the exclusive economic zone, the 200-mile belt where the Law of the Sea treaty gives a coastal country control of resources. So Panama would have had a strong legal say over the platforms. Nothing was built, and the question never came up. It is an early example of a common pattern, in which laws and a flag are easy to produce and a billion dollars is not.

seasteading-institute.story:
A seastead is a permanent home at sea. The Seasteading Institute is an American non-profit that promotes them, founded on 15 April 2008 by Wayne Gramlich and Patri Friedman because they wanted room to try new forms of government. The basic argument comes from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. A country's exclusive economic zone, where it controls resources, runs 200 nautical miles from shore. Beyond it lie the high seas, which fall under no country's law apart from that of a ship's flag state, the country it is registered in. The founders proposed using that space.

Peter Thiel, a co-founder of PayPal, gave $500,000. The founders hoped to float a prototype in San Francisco Bay by 2010 and a seastead by 2014, and they met neither target. In January 2009 the institute patented ClubStead, a design for a 200-person resort about the size of a city block. In July 2009 Friedman launched Ephemerisle, a floating gathering in the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta inside California, which continued without him.

The institute later turned to working inside a country's waters, with a government's agreement. On 13 January 2017 it signed a memorandum of understanding, a non-binding agreement, with French Polynesia for a floating island prototype with partial self-rule. This changed the idea a good deal, since a host would now be granting the freedom. After political changes linked to a presidential election, the government pulled out and cut ties on 14 March 2018.

No one lives on an institute seastead. It was still publishing in 2024, promoting safety standards after the death of Samuele Landi, who had planned a floating platform in the Indian Ocean. The institute's history shows the gap between the legal theory, which looks wide open, and the practical needs of waves, money and neighbouring governments. Its one real deal needed permission, and permission was withdrawn.

akon-city.story:
Akon City was a planned futuristic city on the coast of Senegal in West Africa, in the M'bour Department. Its promoter was the singer Akon, born Aliaune Thiam in the United States and partly raised in Senegal. He announced it in June 2018 at the Cannes Lions advertising festival, saying that it would run on his own cryptocurrency, Akoin, and that President Macky Sall had given him 2,000 acres, about 800 hectares.

It was not a claim to independence. It was a special development within Senegal, and its land rested on a deal with the state. On 13 January 2020 Akon signed a memorandum of understanding, a preliminary agreement, with Sapco, Senegal's state tourism development body, in the presence of the tourism minister. A groundbreaking ceremony followed in August 2020. The reported cost was $6 billion, to come mainly from American private partners, with a first phase by 2023 and completion by 2029. Commentators compared the curving tower designs with Wakanda from the Black Panther films.

The city did not appear on schedule. A welcome centre was under construction at the site in December 2023. In 2025 the head of Sapco, Serigne Mamadou Mboup, told the BBC that the Akon City project no longer exists. He said Akon and Sapco had agreed on a more realistic project that Sapco would support.

A government's backing and a famous name gave this project attention, but they did not produce the money. Since the land came through a state agency, the agency could change the deal when nothing was built. The city's private money and its private currency could not change that, because its legal base was a preliminary paper with the Senegalese state.

bitcoin-city.story:
El Salvador is a small Central American country. In 2021 its president, Nayib Bukele, made bitcoin, a digital currency, legal tender, meaning money that businesses had to accept. In November 2021 he announced Bitcoin City, a planned city in La Unión at the foot of the Conchagua volcano. Geothermal power from the volcano was to be used for mining bitcoin, the computer process that creates new coins. The city was to be circular, like a coin. The Mexican architect Fernando Romero showed models of its airport with Bukele in 2022.

The plan was for a place of low tax inside a country, set up by that country's own government. It would have almost no taxes apart from a 13 percent value-added tax, a sales tax, half of which would pay off bonds. Money was to come from a $1 billion "volcano bond" involving the state power company LaGeo, with half for the city and half for buying bitcoin. Some bond buyers might receive Salvadoran citizenship.

A plan like this needs lenders. NBC reported that analysts paid more attention to the bonds than to the city, and delays in financing and construction followed. Then the larger lender acted. Under a later deal with the International Monetary Fund, a global lender to governments in financial trouble, businesses no longer had to accept bitcoin and taxes could no longer be paid in it. The Week described this as ending bitcoin's run as effective legal tender. A government that needs outside credit can find its own policy altered as a condition of the loan.

An airport in the plan was expected to start operating in 2027, according to a 2025 source. The city itself is not known to have been built. Compared with private projects, Bitcoin City had every legal advantage, since a sitting president could simply decree the rules. It still needed money and a country's finances that could carry the plan.

cheran.story:
Cherán is a town of the Indigenous Purépecha people in the state of Michoacán, in western Mexico. Its economy rests on timber, and Mexico's cartels had moved into logging. For more than three years armed loggers and masked men demanding money from small businesses worked there without being punished, and killings and kidnappings became routine. Trucks full of cut logs passed through the town day after day. By 2011 the loggers were getting close to one of the town's water springs, and water was what finally moved people.

A group of local women met in secret. They decided to stop the trucks in town, where neighbours could back them up. When they did, the uprising drove out the loggers, the police and the politicians.

Then the town had to run itself. Political parties were banned, and they were still banned when the BBC visited five years later. Each of the four districts elected representatives to a ruling council. Armed checkpoints went up on the three main roads, staffed by the Ronda Comunitaria, a local force of men and women who stop every vehicle and question those inside.

The important legal step came next. The community asked to choose its authorities by its own customs, and on 2 November 2011 Mexico's federal Electoral Tribunal ordered Michoacán's electoral authority and state congress to act on that request. The court's order turned a local uprising into an arrangement that the state had to deal with. The town is now described as a self-ruling Indigenous community largely free of the crime and corruption that caused the revolt.

Cherán does not claim to be a separate country. That is a large part of why it survives. It asked to be governed differently within Mexico, on the grounds of existing rights, and it won that in a Mexican court. It offers a contrast with many declared states. It has real land, real residents and real day-to-day control, and it did not need a flag or passport to get them.

difc.story:
Many people who want a separate legal territory actually want better commercial law and lower tax. The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) shows a government providing exactly that. It is a 110-hectare business district in Dubai, one of the emirates that make up the United Arab Emirates, with its own commercial law and courts.

Its creators wanted to attract international finance, and bankers and investors prefer legal systems they know. In September 2004 a federal law allowed each emirate to set up legal structures for financial centres. Dubai Law No. 9 of 2004 then created the centre, and Dubai Law No. 12 created its courts, which began working in 2006. Inside the zone, civil and commercial cases follow common law, the English system built on past court rulings, in English, separately from the rest of the country's legal system.

It also has its own financial regulator and offers companies a 50-year guarantee of zero tax on corporate income. Other laws, such as criminal law and immigration rules, still apply there. So a banker in the DIFC can sign a contract governed by the zone's commercial law, but if arrested for assault is dealt with under the national criminal system.

At first the courts could hear only cases tied to the zone. A law of 31 October 2011 let them hear any local or international commercial case if all parties agree, so firms with no link to the zone can also use them. In effect the courts became a service open to anyone who chooses them.

The zone remains part of Dubai, and its courts are part of the emirate's own structure. Its powers come from statutes, so they could be changed by further statutes. No one here claims independence. The case shows how far a country can go in carving out a separate legal system, and shows that the carving is done by the country.

forest-city.story:
Forest City is a $100 billion housing project on the coast of Johor, Malaysia, about a 30-minute drive from Singapore. The Chinese developer Country Garden started it in 2016 and marketed it mainly to buyers in mainland China as a luxury home for 700,000 people.

It did not fill up. Country Garden told Bloomberg that 9,000 people lived there, while the magazine Domus reported in July 2024 that just over 1 percent of the development was thought to be inhabited. Business Insider reported that the company owed over $190 billion.

Malaysia then stepped in. On 20 September 2024 it launched a Special Financial Zone covering the area, with tax breaks from early 2025. They included a zero rate for family offices, private firms that manage the wealth of rich families, and lower personal income tax for some people who move there. Analysts quoted by BenarNews disagreed on whether this would work. The area also briefly housed the Network School, a community of tech workers inspired by the idea of founding new countries online, until the local council revoked its business licence in July 2026.

Forest City never sought sovereignty. It stays under Malaysian law with a state-backed tax arrangement, and it is included as a comparison. A huge private development remains an ordinary piece of a country, and the tax rules it depends on can be granted or changed by that country's government.

aisland-landi.story:
Samuele Landi was an Italian businessman whose company, Eutelia, went bankrupt in 2010. He was tried for fraud in Italy and sentenced in his absence to 14 years, and he moved to Dubai. The reporter Ian Urbina of the Outlaw Ocean Project writes that Landi avoided extradition, the handing over of a suspect to another country, and obtained diplomatic credentials from Liberia. He then decided to start his own country at sea.

His target was the Saya de Malha Bank, a huge underwater plateau in the Indian Ocean, among the largest in the world and less than 33 feet deep in places. Most of it lies in international waters, hundreds of miles from any country's coast. It had attracted such dreams before. In 1997 the architect Wolf Hilbertz and the marine biologist Thomas Goreau sailed there from the Seychelles to begin building a micronation called Autopia.

Landi began closer to home. He bought an 800-ton flat barge, anchored it about 30 miles off Dubai in the Persian Gulf, and bolted six shipping containers to the deck as living quarters, with solar air conditioning and a machine to make fresh water from seawater. He called it Aisland. He lived aboard for over a year with three sailors, a cook and five cats, raising money for a larger barge to take to the bank. He hoped for about twenty barges and thousands of residents by 2028, and planned to mount a Gatling gun against pirates.

Safety was the problem. The Seasteading Institute says a captain warned him that the barge was unsafe. No flag state, the country whose rules a vessel sails under, or inspection body is known to have checked it. On 2 February 2024 a wave broke it in two. Two crew members survived by clinging to wood until a passing ship picked them up the next day. Landi and two employees, named as Abdul and Javed Khan, died, and his body came ashore about 40 miles up the coast.

The project ended with his death. It is the clearest case of what escaping all rules also means. The inspectors and coast guards that a seasteader wants to avoid are the same services that check a hull and answer a distress call, and the risk fell on employees as well as on the man who chose it.

bakov-arca-noe.story:
Anton Bakov is a Russian businessman and former member of Russia's parliament who chairs the Monarchist Party. He is known for a long series of unusual political projects, including a local currency called the Ural franc. In 2011 he founded a project to restore the Russian Empire, overthrown in 1917, as a small state somewhere outside Russia.

Under the name Imperial Throne it issued a manifesto on 31 March 2014 naming a German prince, Karl Emich of Leiningen, as Emperor Nicholas III, with Bakov as prime minister and later Archchancellor. It took the name Romanov Empire in 2017. It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about 31 American dollars, and claimed about 4,000 by 2014. In 2013 it said it had given citizenship to Edward Snowden, the American who leaked secret surveillance files.

Because a state needs land and it had none, its leaders went shopping. Nicholas III asked Vladimir Putin for land in Yekaterinburg and was refused. Bakov held talks to buy territory from Kiribati and the Gambia, and these had failed by 2017.

In 2020 Bakov announced a successor project called Arca Noë, to be based in what he called neutral Mediterranean waters close to Venice, as part of the seasteading movement, which aims to build permanent homes at sea. No structure has been reported.

The search shows the usual progress of a claim without land. It starts with asking governments, and after they refuse it moves to open water, where no state's consent seems necessary, and building there has its own costs. So the project remains a title, a set of passports and a plan.

freetown-christiania.story:
Freetown Christiania is a self-governing community of about 900 people on the site of an old military barracks in the Christianshavn district of Copenhagen, Denmark. It shows how a squat in the middle of a capital city can last more than fifty years, and on what terms.

In 1971 squatters moved in. They set up a community with free cannabis, little government, no cars and no police, and an article in a local paper proclaimed a free town. Decisions are made at residents' meetings and in working groups. The Defence Ministry sued in 1976, and the Supreme Court ruled on 2 February 1978 that the site should be cleared at once. Later governments did not carry out the order.

The most persistent conflict was Pusher Street, the main lane, known for its open sale of hashish, which is illegal in Denmark. Later governments tried to close the community, often over this trade. After hard talks, residents agreed in June 2011 to set up a fund to buy the land. With the first payment in July 2012 they became legal owners of part of it, and the rest stayed with the state. A foundation, Foundation Freetown Christiania, now runs the area.

This changed the footing. A squatter has no title, while a landowner has one, but a landowner also pays bills and answers to the same laws as everyone else. After repeated shootings, residents and authorities together dug up Pusher Street on 6 April 2024, which unlocked state money for renovation and for joining the area to the wider city. In February 2026 residents reluctantly accepted a public housing plan for about 300 people, with building possibly starting around 2029, and some residents fear that newcomers could change the character of the place.

Christiania draws half a million visitors a year and remains under Danish law. No state recognises it as independent, and the Danish state has dealt with it mainly by negotiating. It kept its land by staying in Denmark, using tolerance and then purchase. Each step has brought it closer to ordinary Danish life.

maldives-floating-city.story:
The Maldives is a low-lying island nation in the Indian Ocean, threatened by rising seas. Maldives Floating City is a planned housing project on a 200-hectare lagoon about 10 minutes by boat from Malé, the capital. Homes that float would rise with the water, which is the main reason it is promoted. The design by the Dutch firm Waterstudio, under the architect Koen Olthuis, uses a pattern like brain coral, with about 5,000 units, including houses, shops and schools, for about 20,000 people.

The government signed the deal with the Dutch developer Dutch Docklands in 2010. It stalled after a change of government in February 2012 and was signed again on 8 May 2019, when five lagoons were allotted to the company. The deal was revised on 23 June 2022. A ministry reply reported by Atoll Times said that no work had begun on the lagoons, none had been reclaimed and two had been sold, and Economy Minister Fayyaz Ismail called the project a scam.

In June 2023 the company said the plan had changed at the government's request, with first prices lowered to about $100,000, work starting that August and completion in early 2028. Reports differ on progress. One said no mockup had been shown despite three announced dates, and a February 2023 report said a mockup could be seen in the Hulhumalé lagoon. In May 2024 Newsweek published satellite images it described as showing construction, and Olthuis expected first residents within 14 months. Other accounts give an opening in 2027. Finished homes or residents have not been confirmed.

The legal position is simple. The project rests on lagoon leases from the Maldives government, inside Maldivian waters, under Maldivian law, and it can be renegotiated by each new government, as it has been. It is included because floating homes are often linked with escape from national law. Here a floating city is an ordinary real estate deal in which the state is landlord, and in which the state's politics have shaped each stage.

mount-athos.story:
Mount Athos is a 335-square-kilometre mountainous peninsula in northern Greece, on the Aegean Sea, home to 20 Orthodox Christian monasteries. Monks have lived there since at least the 9th century. It is one of the oldest examples of a community governing itself inside a modern state.

Most of the peninsula is run as a self-governing region of Greece by the monks themselves. In church matters it answers to the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, the senior bishop of Orthodox Christianity. The rest of the peninsula belongs to an ordinary Greek municipality.

Its best-known rule is the exclusion of women. A 10th-century charter bars female animals, and Greek law and religious tradition exclude women, who may not come within 500 metres of the coast. Dr Graham Speake, an author on Athos, told the BBC that the charter did not mention women because everyone already knew they were not allowed in men's monasteries. Tradition also holds that the Virgin Mary was blown off course and landed there, and that the mountain was set aside for her alone. The BBC described it as perhaps the largest area in the world from which women are barred.

The monks also control who comes in, much as a state controls its border. A man sends a copy of his passport to the Pilgrims' Bureau, and each day 100 Orthodox and 10 non-Orthodox men are admitted for three nights in one of the monasteries. They board a ferry from one of two nearby ports. Women are refused a permit. Vladimir Putin has visited to mark 1,000 years of Russian monks there. UNESCO, the United Nations cultural agency, listed the site in 1988.

Athos is an example of very long-lasting self-rule that makes no claim to be a country. Its special status rests on Greek law, which recognises it, and it remains part of Greece. A group looking for this kind of arrangement would note what it took, which was more than a thousand years of history and a religious role that the surrounding state respects.

prospera-zede.story:
Próspera is a private business zone with its own rules on Roatán, a Caribbean island off the north coast of Honduras. It is the most fully developed recent attempt to get a country to hand over lawmaking to a private company, and its fate is being decided in court.

The legal path began in Honduras's own politics. An earlier plan, called Special Development Regions, was struck down as a breach of sovereignty, the country's right to govern itself. In 2013 Honduras changed its constitution to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development (ZEDEs), areas with their own laws, courts and taxes.

Erick Brimen, a Venezuelan-born fund manager, applied in 2017 and built Próspera with American venture capital, through a Delaware company that holds a veto on its council. It offers single-digit taxes, its own regulations and a court of retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Neighbours in the village of Crawfish Rock feared losing their land, and the project became a national issue.

Politics then turned. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, saying Honduras was recovering its sovereignty. On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the ZEDE laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect, which means that they count as invalid from the start.

Its owners had already claimed about $10.8 billion from Honduras at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), a World Bank body that decides disputes between investors and governments. They relied on a legal stability agreement promising fixed rules and on CAFTA-DR, a trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries. Honduras left ICSID in August 2024, then rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026. Honduran officials said in October 2025 that the claim had dropped to $1.63 billion. The case was still pending in October 2026, when the tribunal issued an order about a site visit, and the zone continues to operate during the dispute.

The case teaches what such a grant is worth. A country can give away lawmaking powers, and a later government and its courts can take them back. What the company holds is a right to seek money, under a treaty, if the taking breaks a promise. That is a large threat for a poor country, and critics and supporters disagree over whether it should exist. It does not amount to sovereignty for the zone.

sark.story:
Sark is a small island in the Channel Islands, off the coast of Normandy, with about 500 people on 5.44 square kilometres, counting the neighbouring islet of Brecqhou. Cars are banned from its roads, and people use tractors, bicycles and horse-drawn carts. It is part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing Crown Dependency, a territory that belongs to the British Crown but is not part of the United Kingdom. It had a form of government that stayed feudal into the 21st century, and that is why it is here.

In 1565 Queen Elizabeth I granted it to Helier de Carteret, of Jersey, as a fief, land held from the Crown in return for service. His conditions were to clear out pirates and keep at least 40 loyal men there, so he rented out 40 plots called tenements. The arrangement stuck. The island's parliament, Chief Pleas, long consisted of the Seigneur, or feudal lord, the Seneschal, a judge, the 40 tenement holders and 12 elected deputies. So most seats went with land ownership. Its laws are based on Norman law.

The challenge came from outsiders who bought in. The billionaire brothers David and Frederick Barclay bought Brecqhou in 1993. In the mid-1990s they went to the European Court of Human Rights to challenge Sark's inheritance law, which required their island to pass to David's eldest son. Women gained equal inheritance rights in 1999. The brothers then argued that the whole system broke the European Convention on Human Rights, the treaty that protects basic rights in Europe. It was replaced under a new constitution in 2008. Sark stopped being a royal fiefdom. Candidates backed by the brothers' businesses won few seats in the elections of 2008 and 2010.

Sark is a useful counterexample for anyone drawn to old charters and private islands. Its self-rule was real and lasted over four centuries, yet the rules of the larger legal system still reached it. Owning a small island gave the Barclays private land and a court case, and it gave them no power to run the place.

vatican-lateran-treaty.story:
Vatican City is the world's smallest state, a 44-hectare walled area inside Rome. It is the leading example of a tiny state created by agreement.

For centuries popes ruled central Italy directly as the Papal States. Italian forces captured Rome in 1870, as Italy unified. Italy's Law of Guarantees of 1871 offered the pope use of the Vatican and Lateran palaces and 3,250,000 lire a year, but no sovereignty, meaning no independent right to rule. The Holy See, the Pope's government, refused, because accepting would have meant being a guest of Italy. Each pope after that called himself a prisoner in the Vatican. This dispute, called the Roman Question, stayed open for about 60 years.

On 11 February 1929, at the Lateran Palace, the Holy See under Pius XI and Italy under King Victor Emmanuel III and Benito Mussolini signed the Lateran Pacts. The treaty recognised the Holy See's full sovereignty over the newly created State of Vatican City, and a financial agreement settled claims over lost land. Italy's 1948 constitution recognised the treaty, and a 1984 revision ended Catholicism's status as the sole state religion.

The state works in an unusual way. Vatican City had 882 residents in 2024. The Pope rules it. It exists to give the Holy See, itself a sovereign body with diplomatic relations around the world, a physical base that no other state controls.

Founders of new territories sometimes point to it as proof that a state can be very small, and that is correct. Its size was never what made it work. The Vatican had many centuries of history, a global church and a claim to lost territory that Italy wished to settle. Most of all, it had the signature of the country surrounding it. A treaty with the neighbouring state is the cleanest way to create a new state, and that consent is what nearly every other case here lacks.

haudenosaunee-passport.story:
A passport normally comes from a state that other states recognise. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy, also called the Iroquois, is an alliance of Indigenous nations in New York State and Canada, including the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and Tuscarora. It regards itself as sovereign, and it has issued its own passports since at least 1923. That year one went to the Cayuga statesman Deskaheh so that he could travel to the League of Nations in Geneva to argue his people's case. The modern form has been used since 1977.

The Haudenosaunee case differs from a self-declared micronation's. It is a real people on their own lands, with a long-standing political body. Using the document is a statement of sovereignty as well as a way to travel. 

Other countries treat it unevenly, as each border is its own decision. Japan admitted a delegation on it in 2005. In early 2010 a delegation from Kahnawake was stranded in El Salvador for weeks trying to return on it. In July 2010 Britain refused it for the Haudenosaunee lacrosse team travelling to the World Championship, and the United States offered the players American passports, which they rejected. The team's director called the Haudenosaunee the originators of the game. Israel accepted the team's passports in July 2018, subject to Canadian assurances that they could return, after trouble boarding a flight in Toronto. The team cleared customs in Tel Aviv on 12 July, hours before its first game against the United States. Ireland accepted them in August 2022.

The Israeli condition points to the practical heart of the matter. A country admitting a traveller wants to know where that person can be sent back to, and only a recognised state usually answers that question. The European Union and the Isle of Man list the document as a "fantasy passport", one issued by a body they do not treat as a state. The United States, British and Canadian governments have refused to endorse it, and it is not accepted for entry into Canada.

It is still issued and still judged case by case. The passport shows that a people can keep a claim to nationhood alive through a document for a century, and that their ability to use it depends on decisions made at each foreign border.
